chapters.title: SIMILAR SOLIDS
chapters.text_markdown:
Two right circular cylinders are *similar* if they are generated by similar rectangles revolving about corresponding sides.
379.I. If in two similar cylinders $s$ and $s'$ are the lateral areas, $S$ and $S'$ the total areas, $V$ and $V'$ the volumes, $h$ and $h'$ the altitudes, and $r$ and $r'$ the radii, then $$\dfrac{s}{s'} = \dfrac{S}{S'} = \dfrac{r^2}{r'^2} = \dfrac{h^2}{h'^2} \text{ and } \dfrac{V}{V'} = \dfrac{r^3}{r'^3} = \dfrac{h^3}{h'^3}.$$
**Suggestions for Proof**: To find the ratios $\dfrac{s}{s'}$ and $\dfrac{S}{S'}$, make use of the following, giving reasons for each in detail.
------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------- (1)$s = 2\pi rh$, (2)$S = 2\pi r(r + h)$, (3)$\dfrac{r}{r'} = \dfrac{h}{h'}$, (4)$\dfrac{r + h}{r' + h'} = \dfrac{r}{r'} = \dfrac{h}{h'}$. ------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------
To find the ratio $\dfrac{V}{V'}$ make use of $V = \pi r^2h$, and $V = \pi {r'}^2h'$, and $\dfrac{r}{r'} = \dfrac{h}{h'}$. Two right circular cones are *similar* if they are generated by two similar right triangles revolving about corresponding sides.
381.II. If in two similar cones $s$ and $s'$ are the lateral areas, $S$ and $S'$ the total areas, $V$ and $V'$ the volumes, $h$ and $h'$ the altitudes, and $r$ and $r'$ the radii, then $$\dfrac{s}{s'} = \dfrac{S}{S'} = \dfrac{r^2}{r'^2} = \dfrac{h^2}{h'^2} \text{ and } \dfrac{V}{V'} = \dfrac{r^3}{r'^3} = \dfrac{h^3}{h'^3}.$$
**Suggestions for Proof**: See suggestions under § .
The lateral area of a cone is $36$ square inches. What is the lateral area of a similar cone whose altitude is $\tfrac{3}{4}$ that of the given cone? The total area of one of two similar cones is three times that of the other. Compare their altitudes and also their radii. The sum of the total areas of two similar cones is $144$ square inches. Find the area of each cone if one is $1\tfrac{3}{4}$ times as high as the other. The volume of one of two similar cones is $5$ times that of the other. Compare their altitudes.
Two polyhedrons are *similar* if they have the same number of faces similar each to each and similarly placed, and have their corresponding polyhedral angles equal. Any two parts which are similarly placed are called *corresponding parts*, as corresponding faces, edges, vertices.
383.III. Two tetrahedrons are similar if three faces of one are similar respectively to three faces of the other, and are similarly placed.
To prove $P-ABC \sim P'-A'B'C'$. : (1) Show that $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle A'B'C'$. (2) Show that trihedral $\Angles P$ and $P'$ are equal. Likewise $\angle A = \angle A'$, $\angle B = \angle B'$, $\angle C = \angle C'$. Hence, by definition, the polyhedrons are similar.
If the two prisms in the figure are similar, name the pairs of corresponding parts. Likewise for two similar pyramids.
384.IV. The volumes of two tetrahedrons, having a trihedral angle of the one equal to a trihedral angle of the other, are proportional to the products of the edges which meet in the vertices of these angles.
To prove that $\dfrac{V}{V'} = \dfrac{PA \cdot PB \cdot PC}{P'A' \cdot P'B' \cdot P'C'}$. : Place $P'-A'B'C'$ so that Tri. $\angle P'$ coincides with Tri. $\angle P$. Let $CM$ and $C'M'$ be the altitudes of $P-ABC$ and $P-A'B'C'$ from the vertices $C$ and $C'$ upon the plane $PAB$. Let $AN$ and $A'N'$ be the altitudes of the $\triangles PAB$ and $PA'B'$. Then $\dfrac{V}{V'} = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{3} CM \cdot \text{area } PAB} {\tfrac{1}{3} C'M' \cdot \text{area } PA'B'} = \dfrac{CM \cdot PB \cdot AN}{C'M' \cdot PB' \cdot A'N'}$. Now prove $\dfrac{CM}{C'M'} = \dfrac{PC}{PC'}$ and $\dfrac{AN}{A'N'} = \dfrac{PA}{PA'}$. Hence, we have $\dfrac{V}{V'} = \dfrac{PC \cdot PB \cdot PA}{P'C' \cdot P'B' \cdot P'A'}$. Give all the steps and reasons in detail.
385.V. The volumes of two similar tetrahedrons are in the same ratio as the cubes of their corresponding edges.
To prove that $\dfrac{V}{V'} = \dfrac{\overline{PA}^3}{\overline{P'A'}^3}$. : We have $\dfrac{V}{V'} = \dfrac{PA \cdot PB \cdot PC}{P'A' \cdot P'B' \cdot P'C'}$. §  Now use the properties of similar triangles to complete the proof. Use the figure of § .
Show that two tetrahedrons are similar if they have a dihedral angle of one equal to a dihedral angle of the other and the including faces similar each to each and similarly placed. Show that the total areas of two similar tetrahedrons are in the same ratio as the squares of any two corresponding edges. Show that if each of two polyhedrons is similar to a third they are similar to each other. Two similar tetrahedral mounds have a pair of corresponding dimensions $3$ ft. and $4$ ft. If one mound contains $40$ cu. ft. of earth, how much does the other contain? The edges of a tetrahedron are $3$, $4$, $5$, $6$, $7$, and $8$. Find the edges of a similar tetrahedron containing $64$ times the volume. Find what fraction of the altitude of a tetrahedron must be cut off by a plane parallel to the base, measuring from the vertex, in order that the new pyramid thus detached may have one fifth of the original volume.
Two figures are said to have a *center of similitude* $O$, if for any two points, $A$ and $B$, of the one figure the lines $AO$ and $BO$ meet the other in two points, $A'$ and $B'$, called *corresponding points*, such that $$OA : OA' = OB : OB'.$$ See figures under §§ --.
387.VI. Any two figures which have a center of similitude are similar.
: Given$\dfrac{OA}{OA'} = \dfrac{OB}{OB'} = \dfrac{OC}{OC'}$.
Let the student prove that $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle A'B'C'$. In case the triangles do not lie in the same plane, use §  to show that the corresponding $\Angles$ are equal. Given $\dfrac{OA}{OA'} = \dfrac{OB}{OB'} = \dfrac{OC}{OC'}$, etc.
Give the proof both for polygons in the same plane and not in the same plane.
With the same hypothesis as before, we must prove $\triangle PAB \sim \triangle P'A'B'$, $\triangle PBC \sim \triangle P'B'C'$, $\triangle PCA \sim \triangle P'C'A'$, and then use § . (a) Prove corresponding polygonal faces similar. (b) Prove corresponding polyhedral angles equal. The last step requires not only equal *face angles* about the vertex, as in the case of the tetrahedron, but also equal *dihedral* angles. Note that two dihedral angles are equal if their faces are parallel right face to right face and left face to left face. (Why?) (5)Consider *any two figures whatsoever* having a center of similitude. (a) Take any three points $A$, $B$, $C$, in one figure and the three corresponding points, $A'$, $B'$, $C'$, in the other. Then $AB$ and $A'B'$, $AC$ and $A'C'$, etc., are called *corresponding linear dimensions*, and the triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are *corresponding triangles*. (b) It is clear that any two corresponding linear dimensions have the same ratio as any other two, and that any two corresponding triangles are similar. In this sense any two figures having a center of similitude are thus proved to be *similar*. The *ratio of similitude* of two similar figures is the common ratio of their corresponding linear dimensions. This ratio is the same as the *distance ratio* of corresponding points from the center of similitude.
389.VII. Two similar triangles may be so placed as to have a center of similitude.
To prove that they may be placed with a center of similitude. : From any point $O$ draw $OA$, $OB$, $OC$. On these rays take $A_1$, $B_1$, $C_1$ so that $$\dfrac{OA_1}{OA} = \dfrac{OB_1}{OB} = \dfrac{OC_1}{OC} = \dfrac{A'B'}{AB}.$$ Now show the following: (1)$\triangle T_1 \sim \triangle T$, and hence $\triangle T_1 \sim \triangle T'$. (2)$\triangle T_1 = \triangle T'$. For this show that $A_1B_1 = A'B'$ by means of the equations $$\dfrac{A_1B_1}{AB} = \dfrac{OA_1}{OA} \text{ and } \dfrac{A'B'}{AB} = \dfrac{OA_1}{OA}.$$ Likewise $A_1C_1 = A'C'$ and $B_1C_1 = B'C'$. (3) Finally, $\dfrac{OM_1}{OM} = \dfrac{OA_1}{OA}$, where $M$ and $M_1$ are any two corresponding points. Hence $O$ is the required center of similitude.
390.VIII. Two similar tetrahedrons may be so placed as to have a center of similitude.
To prove that they can be placed so as to have a center of similitude. : With $O$ as a center of similitude, construct $T_1$, making $$\dfrac{OA}{OA_1} = \dfrac{OB}{OB_1} = \text{etc.} = \dfrac{AB}{A'B'}.$$ Now show as in §  that $T_1 = T'$, and hence that $T'$ can be placed in the position $T_1$ so as to have with $T$ the center of similitude $O$. Give all the steps in detail.
391. Any two similar polyhedrons may be placed so as to have a center of similitude.
The argument is precisely similar to that in § .
In the proofs for the two preceding theorems the center of similitude was taken *between* the two figures or *on the same side* of them. The center may be taken equally well *within* them, as in the following illustrations:
In the case of similar convex polyhedrons with the center of similitude thus placed, the faces are the bases of pyramids whose vertices are all at the center of similitude. If, further, the polygonal faces be divided into triangles by drawing their diagonals, these triangles become the bases of tetrahedrons, all of whose vertices are at the center of similitude.
Moreover, each inner tetrahedron is similar to its corresponding outer tetrahedron. (Why?) The volumes of the two similar polyhedrons are thus composed of the sums of sets of similar tetrahedrons.
Give the proof of § , using Fig. 1 above, and extend the argument to two similar polygons, using Fig. 2. Draw two similar tetrahedrons with their center of similitude within them, and give the proof of §  with the figure thus made. Give the proof of § , using Fig. 3 above.
393.IX. The volumes of any two similar polyhedrons are proportional to the cubes of their corresponding edges.
: Place the polyhedrons whose volumes are $V$ and $V'$ so as to have their center of similitude within them as in the third figure of § . Call the volumes of the similar tetrahedrons $T_1$, $T_2$, $T_3$, $\dotsc$, and $T'_1$, $T'_2$, $T'_3$, $\dotsc$, and let $AB$ and $A'B'$ be two corresponding edges. Then we have $$\dfrac{\overline{AB}^3}{\overline{A'B'}^3} = \dfrac{T_1}{T'_1} = \dfrac{T_2}{T'_2} = \dfrac{T_3}{T'_3} = \dotsb. \tag*{(Why?)}$$ And $\dfrac{T_1 + T_2 + T_3 + \dotsb }{T'_1 + T'_2 + T'_3 + \dotsb } = \dfrac{T_1}{T'_1} = \dfrac{\overline{AB}^3}{\overline{A'B'}^3}$.(Why?)\ But $T_1 + T_2 + T_3 \dotsb = V$ and $T'_1 + T'_2 + T'_3 \dotsb = V'$. Hence,$\dfrac{V}{V'} = \dfrac{\overline{AB}^3}{\overline{A'B'}^3}$.
394. The volumes of any two similar solids are proportional to the cubes of any two corresponding linear dimensions.
This proposition may be rendered evident by noticing that any two similar three-dimensional figures may be built up to any degree of approximation by means of pairs of similar tetrahedrons similarly placed. The proposition then holds for any two corresponding figures used in the process of approximation. Note that the ratio of similitude of two similar figures may be obtained from the ratio of any pair of their corresponding linear dimensions. The theorem that any two figures which have a center of similitude are similar is the geometric basis of many mechanical contrivances for enlarging or reducing both plane and solid figures; that is, for constructing figures similar to given figures and having with them a given ratio of similitude.
The essential property of all such contrivances is that one point $O$ is kept fixed, while two points $A$ and $B$ are allowed to move so that $O$, $A$, and $B$ always remain in a straight line, and so that the ratio $OA : OB$ remains the same. See page 216 of Plane Geometry.
In the first figure on this page $O$ is a fixed point. Segments $OD$, $CB$, and the sides of the parallelogram $ACED$ are of fixed length. Prove that if $B$ is once so taken on the line $EC$ as to be in the line $OA$, the points $O$, $A$, and $B$ will always remain collinear, and that $OA : OB$ remains a fixed ratio.
In the second figure is shown an ordinary *pantograph* used for copying and at the same time for reducing or enlarging maps, designs, etc. The lengths of the various segments are adjustable, as shown, thus obtaining any desired scale.
The same contrivance may be used for copying figures in *space*, such as relief maps, and at the same time reducing or enlarging them. Now consider any two similar figures whatever so placed as to have a center of similitude $O$. We have seen that if points $A$, $B$ and $A'$, $B'$ are corresponding points of the two figures, then the ratio of the *corresponding linear dimensions* $AB$ and $A'B'$ is equal to the ratio of similitude $m : n$ of the two figures. Also if $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ and $A'$, $B'$, $C'$, $D'$ are corresponding points, then $\triangles ABC$ and $A'B'C'$, and the tetrahedrons $ABCD$ and $A'B'C'D'$ are similar, and we have $$\dfrac{\text{area } ABC}{\text{area } A'B'C'} = \dfrac{m^2}{n^2} \text{ and } \dfrac{\text{vol.\ } ABCD}{\text{vol.\ } A'B'C'D'} = \dfrac{m^3}{n^3}.$$ The points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ determine two planes, each of which intercepts a certain plane figure in the solid figure to which the points belong. These two plane figures we call *corresponding cross sections*. We assume without full argument:
397.X.  The ratio of the areas of any pair of corresponding cross sections or any pair of corresponding surfaces of similar figures is equal to the square of their ratio of similitude, and  The ratio of the volumes of any two similar figures is equal to the cube of their ratio of similitude.
The fact that the ratio of the areas of corresponding surfaces of similar solids is equal to the *square* of their ratio of similitude, while the ratio of their volumes equals the *cube* of this ratio is one of the most important and far-reaching conclusions of geometry. Thus the ratio of the weights of two similar shells used in gunnery, or the ratio of the weights of two men of similar build, may be found when their ratio of similitude is known.
If it is known that a steel wire of radius $r$ will carry a certain weight $w$, how great a weight will a wire of the same material carry if its radius is $2r$?
The tensile strengths of wires are in the same ratio as their cross-section areas.
Find the ratio of the diameters of two wires of the same material if one carries twice the load of the other; three times the load. In a laboratory experiment a heavy iron ball is suspended by a steel wire. In suspending another ball of twice the diameter a wire of twice the radius of the first one is used. Is this perfectly safe if it is known that the first wire will just safely carry the ball suspended from it? Discuss fully. In two schoolrooms of the same shape (similar figures) but of different size, the same *proportion* of the floor space is occupied by desks. Which contains the larger amount of air for each pupil? If the shells used in guns are similar in shape, find the ratio of the total surface areas of an eight-inch and a twelve-inch shell. Find the ratio of the weights of the shells in the preceding problem, weights being in the same ratio as the volumes. If a man $5$ ft. $9$ in. tall weighs $165$ lb., what should be the weight of a man $6$ ft. $1$ in. tall, if they are similar in shape? What is the diameter of a gun which fires a shell weighing twice as much as a shell fired from an eight-inch gun, supposing the shells to be similar bodies? Supposing two trees to be similar in shape, what is the diameter of a tree whose volume is three times that of one whose diameter is $2$ feet? What is the diameter if the volume is five times that of the given tree? What if it is $n$ times that of the given tree? Assuming that the weights of schoolboys vary as the cubes of their heights, construct a graph representing the relation between their heights and weights, if a boy $5$ feet $9$ inches tall weighs $130$ pounds.
If $w$ represents the number of pounds in weight and $h$ the number of feet in height, $w = kh^3$. From $w = 130$, when $h = 5 \tfrac{3}{4}$, we have $k = .684$. For the purpose of the graph, $k = .7$ is accurate enough.
From the graph constructed in the preceding example find the weight of a boy $5$ feet tall; one $5$ feet $4$ inches; one $5$ feet $6$ inches. Compare with the weights of boys in your class. If a man $6$ feet tall weighs $185$ pounds, construct a graph representing the weights of men of similar build and of various heights. If steamships are of the same shape, their tonnages vary as the cubes of their lengths. The *Mauretania* is $790$ feet long, with a net tonnage of $32,500$. Construct a graph representing the tonnage of steamships of the same shape, and of various lengths. Other ships which at one time or another have held ocean records are: the (former) *Deutschland*, length $686$ ft. and tonnage $16,500$; the (former) *Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse*, length $648$ ft. and tonnage $14,300$; the *Lucania*, length $625$ ft. and tonnage $13,000$ (nearly); and the *Etruria*, length $520$ ft. and tonnage $8000$. By means of this graph decide whether or not these boats have greater or less tonnage than the *Mauretania* as compared with their lengths. Raindrops as they start to fall are extremely small. In the course of their descent a great many are united to form larger and larger drops. If $1000$ such drops unite into one, what is the ratio of the surface of the large drop to the sum of the surfaces of the small drops? The strength of a muscle varies as its cross-section area, which in turn varies as the square of the height or length of an animal, while the weight of the animal varies as the cube of its height or length. Use these facts to explain the greater agility of small animals. For example, compare the rabbit and the elephant. Assuming the velocities the same, the amounts of water flowing through pipes vary directly as their cross-section areas. How many pipes, each $4$ in. in diameter, will carry as much water as one pipe $12$ in. in diameter? What must be the diameter of a cylindrical conduit which will carry enough water to supply ten circular intakes each $8$ feet in diameter? A water reservoir, including its feed pipes, is replaced by another, each of whose linear dimensions is twice the corresponding dimensions of the first. If the velocity of the water in the feed pipes of the new system is the same as that in the old, will it take more or less time to fill the new reservoir than it did the old? What is the ratio of the new time to the old? If two engine plants are exactly similar in shape, but each linear dimension in one is three times the corresponding dimension of the other, and if the steam in the feed pipes flows with the same velocity in both, compare the speeds of the engines. If two men, one $5$ ft. $6$ in. and the other $6$ ft. $2$ in. in height, are similar in structure in every respect, how much faster must the blood flow in the larger person in order that the body tissues of both shall be supplied equally well?
Note that the amount of tissue to be supplied varies as the cube of the height, while the cross-section area of the arteries varies as the square of the height.

\Appendix{II}{PROJECTION OF LINE-SEGMENTS}
\SecToc{\texorpdfstring{\protect\makebox[1em][r]{II.} Applications of Projection}{Applications of Projection}}

\Paragraph{398.}{Length of Projection.} The projection of a line-segment
\index{Plane@\textbf{Plane}!projections upon}
\index{Projection@\textbf{Projection}!of a line-segment}
on a plane was shown in §~\Sref{121} to be another line-segment.
The \emph{length of this projection} will now be computed in terms of
the given line-segment.

\Paragraph{399.}{Cosine of Projection Angle.} The acute angle between a
\index{Angle@\textbf{Angle}!of projection}
\index{Projection angle@\textbf{Projection angle}}
line-segment and a given line on which it is projected is called
the \emph{projection angle}.

If $l$ is the length of a line-segment and $p$ the length of its
projection, then the ratio $p:l$ is called the \emph{cosine of the projection
angle}.

\textit{E.g.}, in \textsc{Fig}.~1, $\dfrac{p}{l} = \text{cosine}\, \angle BAE$.

\begin{center}
\Input{184ab}{\textwidth}
\end{center}

\Paragraph{400.}{Sine, Cosine, Tangent.} In any right triangle $ABC$
\index{Cosine@\textbf{Cosine of an angle}}
\index{Sine@\textbf{Sine of an angle}}
\index{Tangent@\textbf{Tangent}!of an acute angle}
(\textsc{Fig}.~2), either acute angle, as $\angle A$, is the projection angle
between the hypotenuse and the side adjacent to the angle.

Hence the \emph{cosine} of an acute angle of a right triangle is the
\emph{ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse}.

Likewise we define the \emph{sine} of an acute angle of a right triangle
as the \emph{ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse}, and the
\emph{tangent} of an acute angle of a right triangle as the \emph{ratio of the
opposite side to the adjacent side}.

Using the common abbreviations, $\sin$, $\cos$, and $\tan$, we have
in \textsc{Fig}.~2,
\[
\sin A = \dfrac{a}{c},\quad \cos A = \dfrac{b}{c},\quad \tan A = \dfrac{a}{b}. 
\]


\Section{EXERCISES ON SINES, COSINES, TANGENTS}

The sine, cosine, and tangent are of great importance in
many computations. By careful measurement (and in other
ways) their values may be computed for any acute angle, and
a table formed, like that on page~\Pgref{175}.

\noindent\begin{minipage}[b]{\textwidth-1.5in}
\Indent\textit{E.g.}, if $\angle A = 35$° (measured with a protractor), and if we measure
$AC$, $AB$, and $BC$, and then compute the ratios
$\dfrac{a}{c}$, $\dfrac{b}{c}$, and $\dfrac{a}{b}$, we shall find the values of $\sin 35$°,
$\cos 35$°, $\tan 35$°.
\end{minipage}
\hfill\smash{\Input{185a}{1.5in}}

With an ordinary ruler it will not usually be
possible to make these measurements with sufficient
accuracy to obtain more than one decimal
place.

\begin{Exercises}

\item[1.] Using a protractor, construct angles of $10$°, $30$°, $50$°, $70$°,
and by measurement determine the sine, cosine, and tangent
of each.

\noindent\begin{minipage}[b]{\textwidth-1.75in}
\Indent\item[2.] Prove that the cosine of any
given angle is the same, no matter
what point is taken in \emph{either} side
from which to let fall the perpendicular
to the other side. Prove the same for the tangent.
\end{minipage}
\hfill\smash{\Input{185b}{1.75in}}

\item[3.] Show that if the hypotenuse be taken \emph{one decimeter} in
length, then the length of the side adjacent, measured in
decimeters, is the \emph{cosine} of the angle, and the length of the
side opposite is the \emph{sine} of the angle.

\item[4.] Show that if the side adjacent be taken one decimeter in
length, the length of the side opposite, measured in decimeters,
is the \emph{tangent} of the angle.

\item[5.] Without any direct measurement, show how to compute
the three ratios for each of the angles $30$°, $45$°, $60$°.

\begin{Suggestion}
Make use of the fact that if one acute angle in a right
triangle is $30$°, the side opposite it is one half the hypotenuse.
\end{Suggestion}
\end{Exercises}

\vfil

\Section{LENGTH OF PROJECTION OF A LINE-SEGMENT}

\begin{Theorem}{401.}{I.}
The length of the projection of a
line-segment upon a given line is equal to the length of
the line-segment multiplied by the cosine of the projection
angle.
\end{Theorem}

\noindent\begin{minipage}[b]{\textwidth-2.125in}
\Indent\Objective{Given the projection $p$ of the
line-segment $l$ on the line $CD$,
with the projection angle $A$.}
{To prove that $p = l \cos A$.}

\Proof: By definition we have
$\dfrac{p}{l} = \cos A$. Hence, $p = l \cos A$.
\end{minipage}
\kern -0.375in \smash{\raisebox{-0.25in}{\Input{187a}{2.5in}}}


\begin{Exercises}

\Page{177a}

\item[1.] Find the cosines of the angles $35\text{°}\, 30'$, $54\text{°}\, 15'$, $15\text{°}\, 45'$.

\begin{Suggestion}
The cosine of $35\text{°}\, 30'$ lies between $\cos 35$° and $\cos 36$°.
We assume that it lies halfway between these numbers. This assumption,
while not quite correct, is very nearly so for small differences of
angles, as in this case, where the total difference is only one degree.
From the table $\cos 35\text{°} = .819$, $\cos 36\text{°} = .809$. The number midway
between these is~$.814$, which we take as the cosine of $35\text{°}\, 30'$.

This process is called \textbf{interpolation}. A similar process is used for
sines and tangents.
\end{Suggestion}

\item[2.] Find the tangents of the angles $25\text{°}\, 20'$, $47\text{°}\, 45'$, $63\text{°}\, 40'$.

\item[3.] Find the angle whose tangent is $1.74$.

{\small\textit{Solution}.\quad From the table we have $\tan 60\text{°} = 1.73$ and $\tan 61\text{°} = 1.80$.
Hence, the required angle must lie between $60$° and~$61$°. Moreover, the
number $1.74$ is one seventh the way from $1.73$ to~$1.80$. Hence, we
assume the angle to lie one seventh the way from $60$° to~$61$°, which gives
$60\text{°} + \tfrac{1}{7} \times 1\text{°} = 60\text{°} + 9'$ nearly. The required angle is $60\text{°}\, 9'$.}

\item[4.] Find the angles whose sines are $.276$; $.674$; $.437$.

\item[5.] Find the angles whose cosines are $.940$; $.094$; $.435$.

\item[6.] Find the angles whose tangents are $.781$; $1.41$; $3.64$.

\Section{ALTITUDE OF OBLIQUE PRISM OR CYLINDER}

\begin{Theorem}{402.}{II.}
The altitude of an oblique prism
or cylinder is equal to an element multiplied by the
cosine of the angle between the plane of the base and
that of a right section.
\end{Theorem}

\begin{center}
\Input{189a}{0.4\textwidth}
\end{center}

\Objective{Given an oblique prism or cylinder with base $b$ and right section
$c$, and let $BE$ be a perpendicular between the planes of the bases.}{}

Consider the plane determined by $BE$ and the element $AB$.

This plane is $\perp$ to the plane of $b$ and also to the plane of~$c$.
(Why?)

Hence, it is $\perp$ to the line of intersection of the planes of
$b$ and~$c$. (Why?)

Let this plane cut the planes of $b$ and~$c$ in $GD$ and~$FD$
respectively.

Then $\angle D$ is the measure of the dihedral angle between the
planes of $b$ and~$c$. (Why?)
\begin{flalign*}
&\indent \text{\itshape To prove that} & BE &= AB \cdot \cos D. && \\
&\indent \text{\Proof: We have}        & BE &= AB \cdot \cos \angle ABE. && \tag*{Why?} \\
&\indent \text{But}              & \angle D &= \angle ABE. &&\tag*{Why?} \\
&\indent \text{Hence,}                 & BE &= AB \cdot \cos D. &&
\end{flalign*}

\begin{Corollary}{403.}{}
The dihedral angle between the planes of
the base and a right section of an oblique cylinder or prism is
equal to the angle between an element and the altitude.
\end{Corollary}


\begin{Exercises}

\Section{AREA OF THE PROJECTION OF A PLANE-SEGMENT}

\Paragraph{404.}{Projection of a Plane-Segment.} If from each point in
\index{Plane@\textbf{Plane}!-segment}
\index{Projection@\textbf{Projection}!of a plane-segment}
\index{Measurement@\textbf{Measurement}!of surfaces}
the boundary of a plane-segment a perpendicular is drawn to
a given plane, the locus of the feet of these perpendiculars will
bound a portion of the plane, which is called the \emph{projection of
the plane-segment} on the given plane.

\noindent\begin{minipage}[b]{\textwidth-1.75in}
\Indent\begin{Remark}
\text{E.g.}, the plane-segment $A'B'C'$ in the plane
$N$ is the projection of the plane-segment $ABC$
from the plane $M$ upon $N$.
\end{Remark}

\Indent The \emph{angle of projection} is the angle
between the planes $M$ and $N$.
\end{minipage}
\hfill\smash{\Input{191a}{1.5in}}

\begin{Theorem}{405.}{III.}
The area of the projection of a
plane-segment on a plane is equal to the area of the
plane-segment multiplied by the cosine of the projection
angle.
\end{Theorem}

\begin{center}
\Input{191a}{0.4\textwidth}
\end{center}

\Proof: Let the boundary of the given plane-segment $b$ be
any convex polygon or closed curve.

Using a line perpendicular to the given plane as a \emph{generator},
develop a prismatic or cylindrical surface of which $b$
is a section. The given plane will cut this surface in a
right section whose area we denote by~$c$.

Now cut the surface by a plane parallel to~$b$, forming the
upper base $b'$ of a prism or cylinder whose altitude is~$h$, edge~$e$,
and volume~$V$.


Then $c$ is the projection of $b$ upon the given plane, and
$\angle 1 = \angle 2$ is the projection angle.
\begin{flalign*}
&\indent \text{We are to show that} & c &= b \cos \angle 1. &&&& \\
&\indent \text{We know that}        & V &= ce = bh. &&&& \tag*{Why?} \\
&\indent \text{But}                 & h &= e \cos \angle 2. &&&& \\
&\indent \text{Hence,}              & ce &= be \cos \angle 2. &&&& \\
&\indent \text{That is,}            & c &= b \cos \angle 2 = b \cos \angle 1. &&&&
\end{flalign*}

\begin{Remark}
\noindent\begin{minipage}[b]{\textwidth-1.5in}
\Indent\textit{Note}. The foregoing theorem may be proved \emph{directly} in case the
plane-segment is a rectangle with one side parallel
to the line of intersection of the two planes.
In the figure let $S$ be the given rectangle and $S'$
its projection, with $AB \parallel$ to the line of intersection
of the planes in which $S$ and~$S'$ lie, and $\angle 1$
the angle between them.
\end{minipage}
\hfill\smash{\raisebox{-0.5in}{\Input{192a}{1.375in}}}

\begin{flalign*}
&\indent \text{Then}    & S  &= AB \cdot BC && \\
&        \text{and}     & S' &= A'B' \cdot B'C'. && \\
&\indent \text{But}     & AB &= A'B' && \\
&        \text{and}     & BE &= B'C'. && \tag*{Why?} \\
&\indent \text{But}     & BE &= BC \cdot \cos \angle 1 && \tag*{Why?} \\
&        \text{and}     & S' = A'B' &\cdot B'C' = AB \cdot BC \cos \angle 1. && \\
&\indent \text{That is,}& S' &= S \cos \angle 1. &&
\end{flalign*}

In the case of any plane-segment, rectangles may be inscribed in it
in this position and their number increased indefinitely, so that their sum
will approach more and more nearly to the area of the plane-segment,
and in this way it may be shown to any desired degree of approximation,
that the projection of a plane-segment equals the given plane-segment
multiplied by the cosine of the projection angle.
\end{Remark}

\Paragraph{406.}{Ellipse.} An important special case of the theorem of
\index{Ellipse@\textbf{Ellipse}!area of}
§~\Sref{405} is the area of the figure obtained by projecting a circle
upon a plane not parallel to its own plane, nor at right angles
to it. This figure is called an \emph{ellipse}. On page~\Pgref{182} the principle
developed above is used to find the area of the ellipse.


\Section{THE AREA OF AN ELLIPSE}

\Paragraph{407.}{Projection of a Circle.} In the figure two planes, $M$ and
\index{Projection@\textbf{Projection}!of a circle}
\index{Measurement@\textbf{Measurement}!of surfaces}
$M'$, meet in a line $PQ$. The circle $O$ in $M$ has a diameter
$AB \parallel PQ$ and a diameter $CD \perp PQ$.

In projecting the whole figure upon the plane $M'$ the
diameter $AB$ projects into its equal $A'B'$, while $CD$ projects
into $C'D'$ so that $C'D' = CD \cos \angle 1$.

\begin{center}
\Input{193a}{}
\end{center}

\Page{182}
By theorem §~\Sref{405} the area of the ellipse $A'C'B'D'$ equals the
area of the circle $ACBD$ multiplied by $\cos \angle 1$.

Hence, $\pi r^2 \cdot \cos \angle 1$ is the area of the ellipse.

But $r \cos \angle 1 = O'C'$ and $r = O'B'$. \hfill (§~\Sref{401})

Hence, the area of the ellipse is $\pi \cdot O'C' \times O'B'$.

The segments $A'B'$ and $C'D'$ are called respectively the
major and minor axes of the ellipse, and $O'B'$ and $O'C'$ the
semimajor and the semiminor axes. These latter are usually
denoted by $a$ and~$b$.

\textbf{Hence,\qquad\qquad the area of the ellipse is $\pi ab$}.
\index{Ellipse@\textbf{Ellipse}!area of}

\begin{Remark}
Note that when $a$ and $b$ are equal, the ellipse becomes a circle, and
this formula reduces to $\pi a^2$ as it should.
\end{Remark}


\Section{PROBLEMS AND APPLICATIONS}

\Page{183}
\begin{Itemize}

\item[1.] Given a right circular cylinder the radius of whose base
is $6$~inches. Find the area of an oblique cross section inclined
at an angle of $45$° to the plane of the base.

\item[2.] Given an oblique circular cylinder the radius of whose
right section is $10$~inches. Find the area of the base if it is
inclined at an angle of $60$° to the right section.

\item[3.] If an oblique circular cylinder has an altitude~$h$, an element
$e$, radius of right section~$r$, and $\angle A$ the inclination of
the base to the right section, express the volume in two ways
and show that these are equivalent.

\noindent\begin{minipage}[b]{\textwidth-1.5in}
\Indent\item[4.] A six-inch stovepipe has a $45$° elbow
angle, that is, it turns at right angles. (The
angle $CAB$ is called the elbow angle.) Find
the area of the cross section of $AB$. Likewise
if it has a $60$° elbow angle.

\Indent\item[5.] At what angle must the damper in a
circular stovepipe be turned in order to obstruct just half the
right cross sectional area of the pipe?
\end{minipage}
\hfill\raisebox{0.25in}{\Input{194a}{1.5in}}

\begin{Suggestion}
The damper must be turned so that the projection of
the damper upon a right cross section is equal to half that cross section.
\end{Suggestion}

\item[6.] The comparatively low temperature of the earth's surface
near the pole, even in summer, when the sun does not set for
months, is due partly to the \emph{obliqueness} with which the sun's
rays strike the earth. That is, a given amount of sunlight is
spread over a larger area than in lower latitudes.

\begin{Remark}
Thus, if in the figure $D'C$ is a horizontal line, and $D'D$ the direction
of the sun's rays, then a beam of light
whose right cross section is $ABCD$ is spread

\noindent\begin{minipage}[b]{\textwidth-2.25in}
over the rectangle $A'BCD'$.
In other words, a patch of ground
$A'BCD'$ receives only as much sunlight
as a patch the size of $ABCD$
receives when the sun's rays strike it
vertically. $ABCD = A'BCD' \cos \angle 1$.
\end{minipage}
\hfil\smash{\Input{194b}{1.75in}}\hfil
\end{Remark}

\end{Itemize}


\begin{Remark}
Hence, each unit of area in $A'BCD'$ receives $\cos \angle 1$ times as much
light as a unit in $ABCD$.

Hence, to compare the heat-producing powers of sunlight in any latitude
with that at the place where the sun's rays fall vertically, we need
to know how the projection angle, $\angle 1$, is related to the difference in latitude
of the two places.
\end{Remark}

\begin{Itemize}

\item[7.] If $\angle 1 = 30$°, compare the amount of heat received by a
unit of area in $ABCD$ and $A'BCD'$.

\item[8.] What must $\angle 1$ be in order that a unit of area in $A'BCD'$
shall receive only $\tfrac{1}{5}$ as much light as a unit in $ABCD$?

\item[9.] The figure represents a cross section of the earth with an
indication of the direction of the rays of light as they strike
it at the summer solstice when they are vertical at $A$, the
tropic of Cancer. $B$ represents the latitude of Chicago, $C$ the
polar circle, and $P$ the north pole. The angles $PDE$, $CGF$,
$BKH$ represent the projection angle, $\angle 1$, for the various
latitudes. Prove:

\noindent\begin{minipage}[b]{\textwidth-3in}
\begin{align*}
\angle PDE &= \angle POK, \\
\angle CGF &= \angle COK, \\
\angle BKH &= \angle BOK.
\end{align*}

\begin{Remark}
That is, $\angle 1$ for each place
is the latitude of that place
minus the latitude of the
place where the sun's rays
are vertical.
\end{Remark}
\end{minipage}
\hfil\smash{\Input{195a}{2.75in}}\hfil

\item[10.] Find the relative amount of sunlight received by a unit
of area at the tropic of Cancer and at the north pole at the
time of the summer solstice.

\item[11.] Find the ratio between the amount of light received by
a unit of the earth's area at Chicago and at the tropic of

\item[12.] Find the same ratio for the equator and Chicago at the
winter solstice when the sun is vertical at latitude $23\tfrac{1}{2}$°~south.
\Page{184}

\end{Itemize}

The projection of a line-segment on a plane was shown in §  to be another line-segment. The *length of this projection* will now be computed in terms of the given line-segment. The acute angle between a line-segment and a given line on which it is projected is called the *projection angle*. If $l$ is the length of a line-segment and $p$ the length of its projection, then the ratio $p:l$ is called the *cosine of the projection angle*. *E.g.*, in Fig. 1, $\dfrac{p}{l} = \text{cosine}\, \angle BAE$.
In any right triangle $ABC$ (Fig. 2), either acute angle, as $\angle A$, is the projection angle between the hypotenuse and the side adjacent to the angle. Hence the *cosine* of an acute angle of a right triangle is the *ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse*. Likewise we define the *sine* of an acute angle of a right triangle as the *ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse*, and the *tangent* of an acute angle of a right triangle as the *ratio of the opposite side to the adjacent side*. Using the common abbreviations, $\sin$, $\cos$, and $\tan$, we have in Fig. 2, $$\sin A = \dfrac{a}{c},\quad \cos A = \dfrac{b}{c},\quad \tan A = \dfrac{a}{b}.$$ The sine, cosine, and tangent are of great importance in many computations. By careful measurement (and in other ways) their values may be computed for any acute angle, and a table formed, like that on page .
*E.g.*, if $\angle A = 35$° (measured with a protractor), and if we measure $AC$, $AB$, and $BC$, and then compute the ratios $\dfrac{a}{c}$, $\dfrac{b}{c}$, and $\dfrac{a}{b}$, we shall find the values of $\sin 35$°, $\cos 35$°, $\tan 35$°.
With an ordinary ruler it will not usually be possible to make these measurements with sufficient accuracy to obtain more than one decimal place.

405.III. The area of the projection of a plane-segment on a plane is equal to the area of the plane-segment multiplied by the cosine of the projection angle.
: Let the boundary of the given plane-segment $b$ be any convex polygon or closed curve. Using a line perpendicular to the given plane as a *generator*, develop a prismatic or cylindrical surface of which $b$ is a section. The given plane will cut this surface in a right section whose area we denote by $c$. Now cut the surface by a plane parallel to $b$, forming the upper base $b'$ of a prism or cylinder whose altitude is $h$, edge $e$, and volume $V$. Then $c$ is the projection of $b$ upon the given plane, and $\angle 1 = \angle 2$ is the projection angle. $$\begin{flalign*} &\indent \text{We are to show that} & c &= b \cos \angle 1. &&&& \\ &\indent \text{We know that} & V &= ce = bh. &&&& \tag*{Why?} \\ &\indent \text{But} & h &= e \cos \angle 2. &&&& \\ &\indent \text{Hence,} & ce &= be \cos \angle 2. &&&& \\ &\indent \text{That is,} & c &= b \cos \angle 2 = b \cos \angle 1. &&&& \end{flalign*}$$

In the figure let $S$ be the given rectangle and $S'$ its projection, with $AB \parallel$ to the line of intersection of the planes in which $S$ and $S'$ lie, and $\angle 1$ the angle between them.
$$\begin{flalign*} &\indent \text{Then} & S &= AB \cdot BC && \\ & \text{and} & S' &= A'B' \cdot B'C'. && \\ &\indent \text{But} & AB &= A'B' && \\ & \text{and} & BE &= B'C'. && \tag*{Why?} \\ &\indent \text{But} & BE &= BC \cdot \cos \angle 1 && \tag*{Why?} \\ & \text{and} & S' = A'B' &\cdot B'C' = AB \cdot BC \cos \angle 1. && \\ &\indent \text{That is,}& S' &= S \cos \angle 1. && \end{flalign*}$$ In the case of any plane-segment, rectangles may be inscribed in it in this position and their number increased indefinitely, so that their sum will approach more and more nearly to the area of the plane-segment, and in this way it may be shown to any desired degree of approximation, that the projection of a plane-segment equals the given plane-segment multiplied by the cosine of the projection angle.

The segments $A'B'$ and $C'D'$ are called respectively the major and minor axes of the ellipse, and $O'B'$ and $O'C'$ the semimajor and the semiminor axes. These latter are usually denoted by $a$ and $b$. **Hence,the area of the ellipse is $\pi ab$**.
Note that when $a$ and $b$ are equal, the ellipse becomes a circle, and this formula reduces to $\pi a^2$ as it should.

\Paragraph{408.}{Variables and Functions.} It is often useful to think of
\index{Function@\textbf{Function}}
\index{Variables@\textbf{Variables}}
a geometric figure as \emph{varying} in size and shape.

\begin{Remark}
\textit{E.g.}, if a rectangle has a fixed base, say $10$~inches long, but an altitude
which varies from $3$~inches to $5$~inches, then the area varies from $3 \cdot 10 = 30$
to $5 \cdot 10 = 50$ square inches.

We may even think of the altitude as starting at zero inches and
increasing, in which case the area starts at zero and increases continuously.
\end{Remark}

The altitude which we think of as varying at our pleasure is
called the \emph{independent variable}, while the area, being dependent
upon the altitude, is called the \emph{dependent variable}.

The dependent variable is sometimes called a \emph{function} of the
independent variable, meaning that the two are connected by
a definite relation such that, for any definite value of the independent
variable, the dependent variable also has a definite
value.

\begin{Remark}
Thus, in the formula for the area of a rectangle, $a = bh$, if $b$ is fixed
and $h$ varies, then $a$ is a function of $h$, since for every value of $h$ there is
determined a definite value of~$a$.
\end{Remark}

\Paragraph{409.}{Illustrations of Limits.} If a regular polygon is inscribed
\index{Limit@\textbf{Limit}!of a variable}
in a circle of fixed radius, and if the number of sides of the
polygon be continually increased, for instance by repeatedly
doubling the number, then the apothem, perimeter, and area
are all variables depending upon the number of sides. That is,
each of these is a function of the number of sides.

Now the greater the number of sides the more nearly does
the apothem equal the radius in length. Indeed, it is evident
that the difference between the apothem and the radius will
ultimately become less than any fixed number, however small.
Hence we say that the apothem \emph{approaches the radius as a limit}
\index{Approach@\textbf{Approach}}
as the number of sides increases indefinitely.


Similarly the perimeters of the polygons may be made as
nearly equal to the circumference as we please by making the
number of sides sufficiently great.

Hence we may define the circumference of a circle as the
\emph{limit of the perimeter} of a regular inscribed polygon as the
number of sides increases indefinitely.

The circumference of a circle may also be defined as the
limit of the perimeter of a circumscribed polygon as the number
of sides is increased indefinitely.

Likewise we may define the area of a circle as the \emph{limit of
the area} of the inscribed or the circumscribed polygon as the
number of sides is increased indefinitely.

The notion of a limit may be used to define the length of a
line-segment which is incommensurable with a given unit segment.

\begin{Remark}
Thus, the diagonal $d$ of a square whose side is unity is $d = \sqrt{2}$. Hence
$d$ may be defined as the \emph{limit of the variable line-segment} whose successive
lengths are $1$, $1.4$, $1.41$, $1.414$, $\dotsc$.
 
\end{Remark}

In like manner, the length of any line-segment, whether
commensurable or incommensurable with the unit segment,
may be defined in terms of a limit.

\begin{Remark}
Thus, if a variable segment is increased by successively adding to it
one half the length previously added, then the segment will approach a
limit. If the initial length is $1$, and if the successive additions are $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{1}{4}$, $\tfrac{1}{8}$,
$\tfrac{1}{16}$, $\tfrac{1}{32}$, etc., then the successive lengths are $1$, $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{3}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{7}{8}$, $1 \tfrac{15}{16}$, $1 \tfrac{31}{32}$, etc.
Evidently this segment approaches the limit~$2$.

Hence $2$ may be defined as the limit of the variable segment whose
successive lengths are $1$, $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{3}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{7}{8}$, etc., as the number of successive additions
is increased indefinitely.
\end{Remark}

The idea of a functional relation between variables and the
idea of a limit, as illustrated above, are two of the most important
concepts in all mathematics.


\Section{DEFINITION OF A LIMIT}

\Paragraph{410.}{Constant.} A  quantity  which remains fixed in value
throughout a discussion is called a \emph{constant}.
\index{Constant@\textbf{Constant}}

\begin{Remark}
\textit{E.g.}, the base of the rectangle mentioned in §~\Sref{408} is a constant.
\end{Remark}

\Paragraph{411.}{Variable.} A quantity which continuously changes in
\index{Variables@\textbf{Variables}}
value, or which takes on a succession of different values, is
called a \emph{variable}.

\begin{Remark}
\textit{E.g.}, the altitude and the area mentioned in §~\Sref{408} are variables.
\end{Remark}

\Paragraph{412.}{Limit of a Variable.} If a variable may be made to
\index{Limit@\textbf{Limit}!of a variable}
approach a certain constant quantity in such a way that the
difference between the constant and the variable becomes and
remains less than any assignable value, however small, then
the constant is called the \emph{limit of the variable}.

\begin{Remark}
\textit{E.g.}, the fixed circumference of the circle is the limit of the variable
perimeters of the polygons mentioned in §~\Sref{409}.
\end{Remark}

\item[3.] If one tangent to a circle is fixed and another is made to move so
that their intersection point approaches the circle, what is the limiting
position of the moving tangent?    What is the limit of the measure of the

\item[4.] The arc $AB$ of $74$° is the greater of the two arcs intercepted between
two secants meeting at $C$ outside the circle. The points $A$ and $B$
remain fixed while $C$ moves up to the circle. What angle is the limit of
the variable angle formed by the varying secants? What is the limit
of the measure of this angle?

\item[5.] If in the preceding the secants meet within the circle, what is the
limit of their angle and also of the measure of this angle as the intersection
point moves up to the center of the circle?

\end{Sightwork}


\Section{THE INCOMMENSURABLE CASES}

\Paragraph{413.}{The Incommensurable Cases.} We have seen that there
\index{Incommensurables@\textbf{Incommensurables}}
are segments which are \emph{incommensurable}; that is, which have
no common unit of measure,---for instance, the side and the
diagonal of a square.

For \emph{practical purposes} the lengths of such segments are approximated
to any desired degree of accuracy, and their ratios
are understood to be the ratios of these approximate numerical
measures.

But for \emph{theoretical purposes} it is important to consider these
incommensurable cases further; just as in algebra we not only
\emph{approximate} such roots as $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$, $\sqrt{5}$, etc., but we also deal
with these surds as \emph{exact} numbers.

\begin{Remark}
Instances of this kind occur in such operations as
\[
(\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{2})(\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}) = 3 - 2 = 1.
\]
\end{Remark}

While the length of the diagonal of a unit square cannot be
expressed as an integer or as a rational fraction, that is, as the
quotient of two integers, we nevertheless think of such a segment
as having a \emph{definite length}, or what is the same thing, a
\emph{definite ratio} with the unit segment forming the side of the
square.

We now fix our attention on the \emph{incommensurable ratios
themselves}, and the method of determining them, rather than
on the \emph{process of approach} and the practical computation based
on it.

\Paragraph{414.}{Representation by Irrational Numbers.} In general, the
\index{Irrational@\textbf{Irrational}!number}
ratio between any two incommensurable geometric magnitudes
of the same kind may be represented by what is called an
\emph{irrational number}; that is, a number which is \emph{neither an integer
nor a quotient of two integers}.

Examples of irrational numbers are the surds, such as $\sqrt{2}$, 
$\sqrt[3]{5}$, etc., and the number~$\pi$.


\Section{NUMBERS DEFINED BY SEQUENCES}

\Paragraph{415.}{Numbers Defined by Sequences.} The following is a
\index{Approach@\textbf{Approach}}
\index{Sequence@\textbf{Sequence}!numbers defined by}
method for determining any number, whether rational or
irrational. For simplicity it is applied first to the integer~$1$.

Throughout this discussion the expressions ``point on a line''
and ``number'' will be used interchangeably.

\begin{Remark}
\begin{wrapfigure}[3]{r}{2.25in}
\Input{200a}{2in}
\end{wrapfigure}
On a straight line mark a certain point $0$ (zero), and one unit to the
right of it mark another point~$1$. Also
lay off points such that their distances
from $0$ are 
$\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$, $\tfrac{7}{8}$, $\tfrac{15}{16}$, $\dotsc$.

If this sequence of points is carried ever so far, it will never reach the
point~$1$. If, however, we select a point to the left of~$1$, no matter how
near to it, we may always go far enough along this sequence to reach
points between this point and~$1$. That is, $1$~is the limit of the terms of
this sequence. See §~\Sref{412}.
\end{Remark}

The point $1$ has two definite relations to this sequence:

(a)~\textit{Every point of the sequence is to the left of~$1$}.

(b)~\textit{For any fixed point to the left of $1$ there are points of the
sequence between it and~$1$}.

We see that~$1$ is the \emph{only} point on the whole line such that
both (a) and~(b) are true of it. For every point to the right
of~$1$ (a)~is true, but (b)~is not. For every point to the left of~$1$
(b)~is true, but (a)~is not.

It follows therefore that, while the points of the sequence
merely \emph{approach} the point~$1$ as a limit, the sequence, \emph{taken as
a whole, serves to distinguish that point from all other points on
the line}.

\begin{Remark}
In the above sequence, the terms continually \emph{increase}. The number~$1$
may be determined equally well by a \emph{decreasing} sequence. For instance,
the sequence $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{8}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{16}$, $\dotsc$ has the following properties which distinguish
the point~$1$ from all other points on the line.
\end{Remark}

(a)~\textit{Every point of the sequence is to the right of~$1$}.

(b)~\textit{For any fixed point to the right of~$1$ there are points of the
sequence between it and~$1$}.


\Section{LIMIT OF AN INFINITE SEQUENCE}

\Paragraph{416.}{Infinite Sequences.} An endless sequence of either kind
just described is called an \emph{infinite sequence}.

Not every infinite sequence serves to single out a definite
point in the manner shown above. Thus the sequence $1$, $2$, $3$,
$4$, $\dotsc$ fails to do so, because its terms grow large beyond all
bound. Such sequences are said to be \emph{unbounded}, while the
sequences $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$, $\tfrac{7}{8}$, $\dotsc$ and $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{8}$, $\dotsc$ are \emph{bounded}.
\index{Sequence@\textbf{Sequence}!bounded}
\index{Sequence@\textbf{Sequence}!infinite}
\index{Sequence@\textbf{Sequence}!oscillating}
\index{Sequence@\textbf{Sequence}!unbounded}
\index{Limit@\textbf{Limit}!of a sequence}

Again, the sequence $1$, $2$, $1$, $2$, $1$, $2$, $\dotsc$ fails to single out a
definite point. This sequence is said to be \emph{oscillating}, since its
terms increase, then decrease, then increase, etc., while $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$,
$\tfrac{7}{8}$, $\dotsc$ and $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{8}$, $\dotsc$ are \emph{non-oscillating}.

\Paragraph{417.}{Limit of a Sequence.} The number $1$ is said to be the
\index{Bound@\textbf{Bound}!greatest lower}
\index{Bound@\textbf{Bound}!least upper}
\emph{least upper bound} of the sequence $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$, $\tfrac{7}{8}$, $\dotsc$. That is, $1$ is the
\emph{smallest number} beyond which the sequence does not go. $1$ is
also said to be the \emph{limit of the sequence}. See §~\Sref{412}.

Similarly, $1$ is the \emph{greatest lower bound} or the \emph{limit} of the
sequence $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{8}$, $\dotsc$; that is, the \emph{greatest number} such that
the sequence contains no number less than it.
\index{Sequence@\textbf{Sequence}!limit of}

In the manner described above any integer may be determined
by an increasing or a decreasing infinite sequence.

\begin{Remark}
\textit{E.g.}, the number $2$ is the limit of the increasing sequence $1$, $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{3}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{7}{8}$,
$1 \tfrac{15}{16}$, $\dotsc$, or of the decreasing sequence $2 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $2 \tfrac{1}{4}$, $2 \tfrac{1}{8}$, $2 \tfrac{1}{16}$, $\dotsc$.
\index{Sequence@\textbf{Sequence}!decreasing, increasing}
\end{Remark}

Two different sequences, both increasing or both decreasing,
may also define the same number.

\begin{Remark}
\textit{E.g.}, each of the increasing sequences $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$, $\tfrac{7}{8}$, $\tfrac{15}{16}$, $\dotsc$ and $\tfrac{2}{3}$, $\tfrac{4}{5}$, $\tfrac{6}{7}$, $\tfrac{8}{9}$, $\dotsc$
determines the number~$1$.

We notice, however, that no matter what definite number we select in
either of these sequences, there is a number in the other greater than it;
that is, neither sequence contains a number greater than every number in
the other. See §~\Sref{420}.
\end{Remark}

It is apparent that any number may be defined as the limit
of a sequence, and we shall assume the converse, namely, that
any bounded increasing or decreasing sequence has a limit.
\Page{190}


\Section{FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES OF LIMITS}

\begin{Axiom}{418.}{}
\index{Axioms@\textbf{Axioms}}
We now assume that: \textit{Every bounded increasing
sequence has a least upper bound, and every bounded decreasing
sequence has a greatest lower bound}.
\end{Axiom}

This axiom may also be stated:

\textit{Every bounded increasing or decreasing sequence has a limit}.

This axiom simply means that every such sequence singles
out a definite number, rational or irrational, in the manner
discussed on page~\Pgref{190}.

\begin{Remark}
Thus, if we attempt to approximate the square root of $2$, we obtain a
sequence, $1$, $1.4$, $1.41$, $1.414$, $1.4142$, $\dotsc$, having for its limit a \emph{definite
number} represented by $\sqrt{2}$, which corresponds to the length of the diagonal
of a square whose side is unity.

Again, if we attempt to approximate the value of~$\pi$, we obtain a
sequence $3$, $3.1$, $3.14$, $3.141$, $3.1415$, $\dotsc$, having for its limit the definite
number represented by~$\pi$, which is the ratio of the circumference to the
diameter of a circle.
\end{Remark}

\begin{Theorem}{419.}{I.}
Two bounded sequences have the
same limit if they are equal term by term.
\end{Theorem}

\Proof: If the sequences are $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ and $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$, and
if $a_1 = b_1$, $a_2 = b_2$, $a_3 = b_3$, $\dotsc$, then they are one and the same
sequence and hence have the same limit by §~\Sref{418}.

\begin{Remark}
\textbf{Historical Note}.\quad The rigorous treatment of limits has been developed
during the last fifty years. The foundation on which it rests is the theory
of irrational numbers, which itself was placed on a firm basis in the early
seventies.

The Greeks dealt with the incommensurable cases in an interesting
manner. Thus, to prove that two incommensurable ratios are equal they
showed that neither can be less than the other. However, they failed to
make explicit definitions of incommensurables and they did not explicitly
state the fundamental axiom of §~\Sref{418} or its equivalent. Their treatment
would be complete and rigorous if supplemented by the proper definitions
and axioms.
\end{Remark}


\Section{FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES OF LIMITS}

\begin{Theorem}{420.}{II.}
Two increasing bounded sequences
have the same limit if neither sequence contains a number
greater than every number of the other.
\end{Theorem}

Let $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ and $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ denote two infinite sequences
with limits $a$ and~$b$, such that no term of the first sequence is
greater than every term of the second, and no term of the
second is greater than every term of the first.

\textit{To prove that $a = b$}.

\Proof: Suppose that $a$ is not equal to $b$ but is less than~$b$.
Then there must be numbers of the sequence $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ greater
than $a$, since by §~\Sref{415} there are numbers $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, greater than
any fixed number whatever which is less than~$b$. This contradicts
the hypothesis of the theorem, and hence $a$ cannot be
less than~$b$. In like manner we show that $b$ is not less than~$a$.
Hence $a = b$. See §~\Sref{20}.

\begin{Theorem}{421.}{III.}
Two decreasing bounded sequences
have the same limit if neither sequence contains
a number less than every number of the other.
\end{Theorem}

\Proof: The proof is exactly similar to that of Theorem~II.

\begin{Exercises}

\item[1.] Show that the sequences $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$, $\tfrac{7}{8}$, $\dotsc$ and $\tfrac{2}{3}$, $\tfrac{4}{5}$, $\tfrac{6}{7}$, $\dotsc$ have the
same limits.

\item[2.] Show that the sequences $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{1}{4}$, $\tfrac{1}{8}$, $\dotsc$ and $\tfrac{1}{3}$, $\tfrac{1}{5}$, $\tfrac{1}{7}$, $\dotsc$ have the
same limits.

\end{Exercises}

The applications of the theory of limits to geometry consist
chiefly in showing that two numbers are equal because they are
the limits of the same sequence, or of sequences having the
property stated in the theorem of §~\Sref{420} or of §~\Sref{421}.


\Section{APPLICATION OF LIMITS TO PLANE GEOMETRY}

\begin{Problem}{422.}
\index{Commensurable@\textbf{Commensurable}!segments}
\index{Sequence@\textbf{Sequence}!approximating}
On a given segment $AB$ to lay off a
sequence of points $B_1$, $B_2$, $B_3$, $\dotsc$, of which $B$ is the limit,
such that each of the segments $AB_1$, $AB_2$, $AB_3$, $\dotsc$ is
commensurable with a given segment~$CD$.
\end{Problem}

\vspace*{-0.25in}
\begin{center}
\Input{204a}{}
\end{center}
\vspace*{-0.125in}

{\small\textit{Solution}:\quad Using $m_1$, an exact divisor of $CD$, as a unit of measure,
lay off on $AB$ a segment $AB_1$, an exact multiple of $m_1$, such that the
remainder $B_1B$ is less than $m_1$. Then $CD$ and $AB_1$ are commensurable.

Using a unit $m_2$, likewise a divisor of $CD$, and less than $B_1B$, lay off
$AB_2$ such that $B_2B$ is less than $m_2$. Then $AB_2 > AB_1$, and $CD$ and $AB_2$
are commensurable.

Continuing in this manner, using as units of measure segments $m_3$,
$m_4$, $\dotsc$ each an exact divisor of $CD$ and each less than $B_2B$, $B_3B$, $\dotsc$
respectively, we obtain a sequence of segments $AB_1$, $AB_2$, $AB_3$, $\dotsc$, each
greater than the preceding and each commensurable with~$CD$.

If the units $m_1$, $m_2$, $m_3$, $\dotsc$ are so selected that they approach zero as a
limit, it follows that $B$ is the limit point of the sequence $B_1$, $B_2$, $B_3$, $\dotsc$.

If a different sequence of divisors of $CD$, as $m_1'$, $m_2'$, $m_3'$, $\dotsc$, is used,
we obtain a sequence of points $B_1'$, $B_2'$, $B_3'$, $\dotsc$, likewise satisfying the
conditions of the problem.

Any two such sequences of points $B_1$, $B_2$, $B_3$, $\dotsc$ and $B_1'$, $B_2'$, $B_3'$, $\dotsc$
determined as above, are both \emph{increasing} and each is such that \emph{no} point
of it is to the right of \emph{every} point of the other.

Hence, by §~\Sref{420} any two such sequences have the same limit point~$B$.
}

\Paragraph{423.}{Limit of a Sequence of Segments.} If $B_1$, $B_2$, $B_3$, $\dotsc$ is a
\index{Limit@\textbf{Limit}!of segments}
sequence of points on the segment $AB$ having the limit~$B$, then
the segment $AB$ is said to \emph{be the limit of the sequence of segments}
$AB_1$, $AB_2$, $AB_3$, $\dotsc$.


\Section{INCOMMENSURABLE RATIOS}

\Paragraph{424.}{Ratio of Two Incommensurable Segments.} The ratio of
\index{Incommensurables@\textbf{Incommensurables}}
\index{Irrational@\textbf{Irrational}!ratio}
\index{Ratio@\textbf{Ratio}!incommensurable}
two incommensurable segments has not been explicitly defined,
but this may now be done in terms of the \emph{limit of a sequence}.

Consider two incommensurable segments $AB$ and $CD$. Let
$a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ be the lengths of segments each commensurable
with $CD$, forming a sequence whose limit is the segment $AB$,
and let $b$ be the length of the segment~$CD$.

Then $\dfrac{a_1}{b}$, $\dfrac{a_2}{b}$, $\dfrac{a_3}{b}$, $\dotsc$ is an increasing bounded sequence having
a limit which we call~$R$.

If $a_1'$, $a_2'$, $a_3'$, $\dotsc$ are the lengths of segments forming any
other sequence whose limit is $AB$, the sequence $\dfrac{a_1'}{b}$, $\dfrac{a_2'}{b}$, $\dfrac{a_3'}{b}$, $\dotsc$ is
another increasing bounded sequence with limit~$R'$.

By §~\Sref{420} we now know that $R = R'$.

This number $R$ is defined as \emph{the ratio of the incommensurable
segments} $AB$ and~$CD$.
