\Section{APPLICATIONS OF LIMITS TO PLANE GEOMETRY}

\begin{Theorem}{426.}{IV.}
\index{Commensurable@\textbf{Commensurable}!segments}
A line parallel to the base of a
triangle, and meeting the other two sides, divides them
in the same ratio.
\end{Theorem}

\noindent\begin{minipage}[b]{\textwidth-1.75in}
\Indent\Objective{Given the $\triangle ABC$ with $DE \parallel BC$ and
cutting $AB$ and $AC$.}
{To prove that $\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{AE}{AC}$.}

\Proof: Consider the case when $AD$
and $AB$ are incommensurable.

Let $D_1$, $D_2$, $D_3$, $\dotsc$ be a sequence
of points on $AB$ whose limit is~$D$.
Through these points draw parallels
to $BC$, meeting $AC$ in $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$, $\dotsc$.
\end{minipage}
\hfill\Input{206a}{1.75in}

Then $E$ is the limit of the sequence of points $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$, $\dotsc$.

For suppose it is not, and that there is a point $K$ on $AE$
such that there is no point of $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$, $\dotsc$ between $K$ and~$E$.
Draw a line parallel to $BC$ through~$K$, meeting $AB$ in~$H$.

But there are points of the sequence $D_1$, $D_2$, $D_3$, \emph{between} $H$
and~$D$, and hence there must be points of the sequence $E_1$, $E_2$,
$E_3$, $\dotsc$ between $K$ and~$E$, which shows that $E$ is the limit of
the sequence $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$, $\dotsc$.

Then the sequence (1)~$\dfrac{AD_1}{AB}$, $\dfrac{AD_2}{AB}$, $\dfrac{AD_3}{AB}$, $\dotsc$ has a limit~$R$
which, by definition, is the ratio of the segments $AD$ and~$AB$.
\hfill §~\Sref{424}

Similarly, the sequence (2)~$\dfrac{AE_1}{AC}$, $\dfrac{AE_2}{AC}$, $\dfrac{AE_3}{AC}$, $\dotsc$ has a limit
$R'$ which is the ratio of $AE$ to~$AC$.

Now $\dfrac{AD_1}{AB} = \dfrac{AE_1}{AC}$, $\dfrac{AD_2}{AB} = \dfrac{AE_2}{AC}$, $\dfrac{AD_3}{AB} = \dfrac{AE_3}{AC}$, $\dotsc$ §~321, P.~G.

Hence, the two sequences, (1) and~(2), are identical and have
the same limit (§~\Sref{419}). Hence $R = R'$.
\QED


\Section{APPLICATIONS TO PLANE GEOMETRY}

\begin{Theorem}{427.}{V.}
\index{Commensurable@\textbf{Commensurable}!angles, arcs}
In the same circle or in equal
circles the ratio of two central angles is the same as the
ratio of their intercepted arcs.
\end{Theorem}

\vspace*{-0.125in}
\begin{center}
\Input{207a}{0.6\textwidth}
\end{center}
\vspace*{-0.125in}

\Proof: In case the arcs are commensurable the proof is
obvious. For, in that case, the common measure of the arcs
divides each into a number of equal parts, say $m$ and~$n$ respectively,
and these arcs subtend the same number of equal angles
at the center (§~\Sref{244}, Plane Geometry.) Hence the ratio of the
arcs is $m : n$ and the ratio of the angles is also $m : n$.

If the arcs $AB$ and $CD$ are not commensurable, let $AB_1$,
$AB_2$, $AB_3$, $\dotsc$ be a sequence of arcs whose limit is~$AB$, each
arc being commensurable with the arc~$CD$.

Then the sequence $\dfrac{AB_1}{CD}$, $\dfrac{AB_2}{CD}$, $\dfrac{AB_3}{CD}$, $\dotsc$ has a limit $R = \dfrac{AB}{CD}$.

Similarly the sequence $\dfrac{\angle AOB_1}{\angle COD}$, $\dfrac{\angle AOB_2}{\angle COD}$, $\dfrac{\angle AOB_3}{\angle COD}$, $\dotsc$ has
a limit $R' = \dfrac{\angle AOB}{\angle COD}$.

But $\dfrac{AB_1}{CD} = \dfrac{\angle AOB_1}{\angle COD}$, $\dfrac{AB_2}{CD} = \dfrac{\angle AOB_2}{\angle COD}$, $\dotsc$,
as shown above for the commensurable case.

Hence, these two sequences are identical and have the same
limit (§~\Sref{419}). Therefore it follows that $R = R'$.
\QED

\begin{Remark}
\textit{Note}.---The student should note the successive steps in the proofs of
§§~\Sref{426}, \Sref{427}: (a)~Definitions of the incommensurable ratios by means
of infinite sequences; (b)~Proof that these sequences are identical;
(c)~Conclusion that the limiting ratios are equal.
\end{Remark}


\Paragraph{428.}{Products of Irrational Numbers.} If  $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ is a
sequence with limit~$a$, then $ka_1$, $ka_2$, $ka_3$, $\dotsc$ is a sequence whose
limit is \emph{defined} as $ka$ where $k$ is any number.

If $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ and $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ are two sequences with limits
$a$ and~$b$ respectively, then $a_1b_1$, $a_2b_2$, $a_3b_3$, $\dotsc$ is a sequence whose
limit is \emph{defined} as~$ab$.

Similarly if $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$, $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ and $c_1$, $c_2$, $c_3$, $\dotsc$ are
sequences with limits $a$, $b$, $c$, then $abc$ is defined as the limit
of the sequence $a_1b_1c_1$, $a_2b_2c_2$, $a_3b_3c_3$, $\dotsc$.

For a complete treatment it would be necessary to show that
these definitions of multiplication of irrational numbers are
consistent with the rest of arithmetic and also that these new
sequences are such as to determine definite limits. This is
possible but is beyond the scope of this book.

\Paragraph{429.}{Area of a Rectangle.} If the sides of a rectangle are incommensurable
with the unit segment, we \emph{define its area} as
follows:
\index{Measurement@\textbf{Measurement}!of surfaces}

Let $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ be a sequence of rational numbers whose
limit is the altitude~$a$; and let $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ be a sequence whose
limit is the base~$b$.

Then the area of the rectangle is the limit of the sequence $a_1b_1$,
$a_2b_2$, $a_3b_3$, $\dotsc$.

\begin{center}
\Input{208a}{0.4\textwidth}
\end{center}

But by definition the limit of $a_1b_1$, $a_2b_2$, $a_3b_3$, $\dotsc$ is the product
$ab$. Hence we have the theorem:

\begin{Theorem}{430.}{VI.}
\index{Area@\textbf{Area}!of a rectangle}
The area of a rectangle is the
product of its base and altitude.
\end{Theorem}


\Section{APPLICATIONS TO PLANE GEOMETRY}

\Paragraph{431.}{Incommensurable Ratios Related to Two Circles.} In a
\index{Incommensurables@\textbf{Incommensurables}}
\index{Sequence@\textbf{Sequence}!approximating}
circle inscribe a sequence $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, $\dotsc$ of regular polygons,
each having twice the number of sides of the one preceding it.

\noindent\begin{minipage}[b]{\textwidth-1.75in}
\Indent Let the perimeters of these polygons be $p_1$, $p_2$, $p_3$, $\dotsc$ and
their areas $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $\dotsc$. Then the
length $c$ of the circle is defined to be
the limit of the sequence $p_1$, $p_2$, $p_3$, $\dotsc$
and its area $A$ is defined to be the
limit of $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $\dotsc$.

\Indent The sequence of polygons thus inscribed
is called an \emph{approximating
sequence of polygons}.
\end{minipage}
\hfil\Input{209a}{1.5in}\hfil

That these sequences are \emph{increasing}
and \emph{bounded} is obvious from the figure.

\begin{Theorem}{432.}{VII.}
The lengths of two circles are
in the same ratio as their radii, and their areas are in
the same ratio as the squares of their radii.
\end{Theorem}

\Proof: Let the radii of the two circles be $r$ and~$r'$. Denote
the ratio $r':r$ by~$k$. Then $r' = kr$.

Inscribe in one circle an approximating sequence of polygons
with perimeters $p_1$, $p_2$, $p_3$, $\dotsc$ and areas $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $\dotsc$. In the
other circle inscribe a sequence of similar polygons. By
§§~476, 477 (Plane Geometry), the perimeters of the latter are
$kp_1$, $kp_2$, $kp_3$, $\dotsc$ and their areas are $k^2A_1$, $k^2A_2$, $k^2A_3$, $\dotsc$.

By §~\Sref{428}, if the limit of $p_1$, $p_2$, $p_3$, $\dotsc$ is $c$ and the limit of
$A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $\dotsc$ is $A$, then the limits of $kp_1$, $kp_2$, $kp_3$, $\dotsc$, and
$k^2A_1$, $k^2A_2$, $k^2A_3$, $\dotsc$ are~$kc$ and~$k^2A$, respectively.

That is, the ratio of the lengths of the circles is $\dfrac{kc}{c} = k= \dfrac{r'}{r}$
and the ratio of their areas is $\dfrac{k^2A}{A} = k^2 = \dfrac{r'^2}{r^2}$.



\Section{APPLICATIONS OF LIMITS TO SOLID GEOMETRY}

\Paragraph{433.}{Incommensurable Solids.} The areas of curved surfaces,
\index{Incommensurables@\textbf{Incommensurables}}
the volumes of cones, cylinders, and spheres, and even of rectangular
solids involve \emph{incommensurable quantities}. We have
already treated these cases informally and have devised means
for computing them \emph{approximately}.

We now give a formal treatment for logical completeness.

\Paragraph{434.}{Rectangular Parallelopiped.} If the three concurrent
\index{Volume@\textbf{Volume}!as a limit of a sequence}
\index{Measurement@\textbf{Measurement}!of volumes}
edges $a$, $b$, $c$ of a rectangular parallelopiped are incommensurable
with the unit segment, the
volume inclosed is defined as follows:

Let $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ be a sequence of
rational numbers whose limit is the
side~$a$. Let $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ and $c_1$, $c_2$, $c_3$, $\dotsc$
be similar sequences whose limits
are respectively the dimensions $b$ and~$c$.

\noindent\begin{minipage}[b]{\textwidth-1.75in}
\Indent Then the volume is the limit of the
sequence $a_1b_1c_1$, $a_2b_2c_2$, $a_3b_3c_3$, $\dotsc$.

But the limit of this sequence is by
definition the product of the limits of the three sequences
$a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$, $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$, $c_1$, $c_2$, $c_3$, $\dotsc$, or $abc$.
\end{minipage}
\hfill\smash{\raisebox{-0.25in}{\Input{210a}{1.625in}}}

Hence, we have the theorem:

\begin{Theorem}{435.}{VIII.}
The volume of a rectangular
parallelopiped is equal to the product of its three
concurrent edges.
\end{Theorem}

\begin{Exercises}

\item[1.] Give in decimals four terms of a sequence which approximates
the volume of a rectangular parallelopiped whose
dimensions are $2$, $4$, $\sqrt{5}$.

\item[2.] Give in decimals four terms of a sequence which approximates
the circumference of a circle whose radius is $10$~in.;
also of a sequence which approximates the area.

\end{Exercises}


\Section{APPLICATION OF LIMITS TO THE PYRAMID}

\Paragraph{436.}{Triangular Pyramid.} In a triangular pyramid inscribe
a set of prisms in a manner similar to that shown in the figure
of §~\Sref{243}.
\index{Circumscribed@\textbf{Circumscribed}!prism}
\index{Inscribed@\textbf{Inscribed}!prism}
\index{Prism@\textbf{Prism}!inscribed}
\index{Volume@\textbf{Volume}!as a limit of a sequence}
\index{Measurement@\textbf{Measurement}!of volumes}

Call $V_1$ the sum of the volumes of these inscribed prisms.

Using as altitudes one half the altitudes of the first set of
prisms, inscribe a second set the sum of whose volumes is~$V_2$.
Continuing in this manner, we obtain a sequence of sets of
prisms with volumes $V_1$, $V_2$, $V_3$, $\dotsc$. The limit $V$ of this sequence
we define as \textbf{the volume of the pyramid}.

\begin{Remark}
Circumscribed prisms may also be used for defining the volume of a
pyramid, in which, case we get a \emph{decreasing} sequence of volumes
$U_1$, $U_2$, $U_3$, $\dotsc$, with limit~$U$. That $U = V$ follows from the fact that
the sum of the volumes of the circumscribed prisms exceeds that of the
inscribed prisms by the volume of the lowest circumscribed prism, and
this may be made as small as we please.
\end{Remark}

\begin{Theorem}{437.}{IX.}
Two pyramids with the same
altitudes and equivalent bases have equal volumes.
\end{Theorem}

\Proof: Call a sequence of inscribed prisms in one pyramid
$V_1$, $V_2$, $V_3$, $\dotsc$, and in the other $V'_1$, $V'_2$, $V'_3$, $\dotsc$. Since corresponding
sets of these prisms have equal volumes (§~\Sref{200}), that
is, $V_1 = V'_1$, $V_2 = V'_2$, $V_3 = V'_3$, 
$\dotsc$, the theorem follows from
§~\Sref{419}.

\Paragraph{438.}{Convex Closed Curves.} We assume that in a \emph{convex
closed curve} (§~\Sref{202}) it is possible to inscribe a sequence of
\index{Curves@\textbf{Curves}!convex, closed}
polygons $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, $\dotsc$, having perimeters $p_1$, $p_2$, $p_3$, $\dotsc$ and
areas $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $\dotsc$ with limits $p$ and $A$ respectively, and to
circumscribe a sequence of polygons $P'_1$, $P'_2$, $P'_3$, $\dotsc$, having
perimeters $p'_1$, $p'_2$, $p'_3$, $\dotsc$ and areas $A'_1$, $A'_2$, $A'_34$, $\dotsc$ with limits
$p'$ and $A'$ respectively, such that $p = p'$ and $A = A'$.

These limits $p$ and $A$ we now define as \textbf{the perimeter and the
area respectively of the curve}.


\Section{APPLICATION OF LIMITS TO THE CYLINDER}

\Paragraph{439.}{The Cylinder.} Given any cylinder with a convex right
\index{Measurement@\textbf{Measurement}!of surfaces}
\index{Measurement@\textbf{Measurement}!of volumes}
cross-section and an element~$e$. In this cross-section inscribe
a sequence $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, $\dotsc$ of polygons, as in §~\Sref{438}, with perimeters
$p_1$, $p_2$, $p_3$, $\dotsc$ and areas $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $\dotsc$, thus defining the
perimeter $p$ and the area $A$ of the cross-section.

Consider a set of prisms inscribed in this cylinder, of which
$P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, $\dotsc$ are right cross-sections.

Then the areas and the volumes of these prisms are respectively
$p_1e$, $p_2e$, $p_3e$, $\dotsc$ and $A_1e$, $A_2e$, $A_3e$, $\dotsc$.

\textbf{The lateral area and the volume of the cylinder are now defined
as the limits of these sequences}.\quad But by §~\Sref{428} these limits are
equal respectively to $pe$ and~$Ae$.

Hence, we have the theorem:

\begin{Theorem}{440.}{X.}
The lateral area of a cylinder is
the product of an element, and the perimeter of a
right section and its volume is the product of an element
and the area of a right section.
\end{Theorem}

\begin{Exercises}

\item[1.] Prove as above that the volume of any convex cylinder
is equal to the product of its altitude and the area of its base.

\item[2.] Prove that the lateral area of a right circular cone is
equal to half the product of the slant height and the perimeter
of its base.

\item[3.] Prove that the volume of any convex cone is equal to
one third the product of its altitude and the area of its base.

\begin{Suggestion}
The treatment required in these exercises is a very close
paraphrase of the definitions and proof given in §~\Sref{439}. Observe that we
cannot begin to make a proof until we have \emph{defined} the subject matter
of the theorem. That is, we must first define \textbf{the areas and volumes in
question}.
\end{Suggestion}
\end{Exercises}


\Section{APPLICATION OF LIMITS TO THE SPHERE}

\Paragraph{441.}{The Sphere.} Through two points $P$ and $Q$ of a sphere
pass a great circle forming a hemisphere with center~$O$.
\index{Volume@\textbf{Volume}!as a limit of a sequence}

\begin{center}
\Input{213ab}{\textwidth}
\end{center}

Divide $OA$, the radius perpendicular to the plane of the
great circle, into the equal parts $OC$, $CB$, and $BA$. Through
$C$ and $B$ pass planes parallel to the plane of $POQ$, meeting
the sphere in points $D$ and~$E$, respectively.

Construct right circular cylinders with axes $OC$ and $CB$
and radii $CD$ and $BE$. Denote by $V_1$ the sum of the volumes
of these cylinders.

Now divide the radius $OA$ into six equal parts and construct
five cylinders in the same manner as above. Let the sum of
these volumes be $V_2$.

Continuing in this manner, each time dividing $OA$ into
twice as many equal parts as in the preceding, we obtain a
sequence of sets of cylinders and a corresponding sequence
$V_1$, $V_2$, $V_3$, $\dotsc$ of volumes.

We now define the volume of the hemisphere as the limit of
the sequence $V_1$, $V_2$, $V_3$, $\dotsc$.

\Paragraph{442.}{} Construct a right circular cylinder with its base in the
plane of $POQ$ and with radius and altitude both equal to~$OA$.

Denote by $F$ the figure formed by the lower base of the
cylinder, its lateral surface and the lateral surface of the cone
whose base is the upper base of the cylinder and whose vertex
is at $O'$. (See the right-hand figure.)


Draw segments $O'M$ and $O'N$. Let the planes through $C$
and $B$ cut $O'A'$ in $C'$ and $B'$ and $O'M$ in $H$ and $K$.

Now form the cylinder $O'C'H$ whose axis is $O'C'$ and whose
radius is $C'H$. Likewise form the cylinder $C'B'K$.

Let $V'_1$ denote the sum of the volumes of $O'C'D'$ and $C'B'E'$
minus the sum of the volumes of $O'C'H$ and $C'B'K$.

In a similar manner, using the planes which divide $OA$ and
hence $O'A'$ into six equal parts, we form another set of five
cylinders, the sum of whose volumes minus that of the smaller
inside cylinders we denote by $V'_2$.

Continuing in this manner, we obtain a sequence of volumes
$V'_1$, $V'_2$, $V'_3$, $\dotsc$ whose limit $V'$ we define as \textbf{the volume of the
given figure}~$F$.

We now prove that $V_1 = V'_1$, $V_2 = V'_2$, $\dotsc$.

Denote $OA$ by $r$, and note that $O'B' = B'K$.

(1)~$\text{Vol.\ } C'B'E' - \text{Vol.\ } C'B'K
  = \pi C'B'(\overline{B'E'}^2 - \overline{B'K}^2)$ \\
\indent$\phantom{\text{(1)~Vol.\ } C'B'E' - \text{Vol.\ } C'B'K}
  = \pi C'B'(r^2 - \overline{O'B'}^2)$.

(2)~$\text{Vol.\ } CBE
  = \pi CB \cdot \overline{BE}^2
  = \pi CB(r^2 - \overline{OB}^2)$, since \\
\indent$\overline{BE}^2 = r^2 - \overline{OB}^2$. But $OB = O'B'$ and $CB = C'B'$.

Hence, $\text{Vol.\ } CBE = \pi C'B'(r^2 - \overline{O'B'}^2)$.

Hence, $\text{Vol.\ } CBE = \text{Vol.\ } C'B'E' - \text{Vol.\ } C'B'K$.

Similarly we show that
\[
\text{Vol.\ } OCD = \text{Vol.\ } O'C'D' - \text{Vol.\ } O'C'H.
\]

Hence, $V_1 = V'_1$. In like manner $V_2 = V'_2$, $V_3 = V'_3$, $\dotsc$.

Hence, $V = V'$, since they are the limits of the same
sequences.

But the volume of the cylinder $O'A'M$ is $\pi r^3$ and of the cone
whose volume was subtracted, $\tfrac{1}{3} \pi r^3$. That is, the volume of
$F$ is $\tfrac{2}{3} \pi r^3$, and hence that of the hemisphere is $\tfrac{2}{3} \pi r^3$. 

Hence, we have the theorem:

\begin{Theorem}{443.}{XI.}
\index{Sphere@\textbf{Sphere}!volume of}
\index{Volume@\textbf{Volume}!of a sphere}
\index{Measurement@\textbf{Measurement}!of volumes}
The volume of the sphere is $\tfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3$.
\end{Theorem}


Note that the above proof consists essentially in showing
that the area of the circle $BE$ is equal to that of the ring
between the circles $B'E'$ and $B'K$, and that the area of the
circle $CD$ is equal to that of the ring between $C'D'$ and $C'H$
and so on.

Indeed, this theorem and also that of §~\Sref{437} are special cases
of what is known as \textbf{Cavalieri's Theorem}.
\Page{202}

\begin{Theorem}{444.}{XII.}
\index{Cavalieri@\textbf{Cavalieri's theorem}}
If two solid figures  are regarded
as resting on the same plane $b$, and if in every
plane parallel to $b$ the sections of the two figures have
equal areas, the figures have equal volumes.
\end{Theorem}

The proof of this general theorem is more difficult than any
thus far given, inasmuch as it involves sequences which \emph{oscillate};
that is, which are neither constantly increasing nor constantly
decreasing.

\Paragraph{445.}{The Area of the Sphere.} About a sphere of radius $r$
\index{Area@\textbf{Area}!of a sphere}
\index{Sphere@\textbf{Sphere}!area of}
\index{Measurement@\textbf{Measurement}!of surfaces}
\index{Measurement@\textbf{Measurement}!of volumes}
construct a sequence of circumscribed polyhedrons such that
the largest face in each polyhedron becomes as small as we
please when we proceed along the sequence. Let $s_1$, $s_2$, $s_3$, $\dotsc$
be the total surfaces of these polyhedrons. This forms a decreasing
sequence with limit $S$ which we define as \textbf{the surface
of the sphere}.

The volumes of these polyhedrons will be $\tfrac{1}{3}rs_1$, $\tfrac{1}{3}rs_2$, $\tfrac{1}{3}rs_3$, $\dotsc$.
Then the volume $V$ of the sphere is defined\footnote{This definition can be shown to be consistent with that of §~\Sref{441}.}
as \textbf{the limit
of this sequence of volumes}.

\settowidth{\TmpLength}{Hence, by §~\Sref{428}, }
Hence, by §~\Sref{428}, $V = \tfrac{1}{3}rS$. But by §~\Sref{443}, $V = \tfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3$.

\makebox[\TmpLength][l]{Then}$S = \tfrac{3}{r} \cdot \tfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 = 4 \pi r^2$.

Hence, we have the theorem:

\begin{Theorem}{446.}{XIII.}
The area of the sphere is $4 \pi r^2$.
\end{Theorem}


\Section{EXERCISES ON LIMITS}

\begin{Itemize}

\item[1.] In addition to those which are found in the text give
other examples of infinite sequences which do not determine
definite numbers.

\item[2.] Give two increasing sequences which determine the
number~$3$. Show that the theorem of §~\Sref{420} applies and proves
that these sequences determine the same number.

\item[3.] Give two decreasing sequences each of which determines
the number~$5$. Apply §~\Sref{421} to show that these sequences
determine the same number.

\item[4.] State fully the relation between a bounded increasing
sequence and the number determined by it. State also the
relations between a bounded decreasing sequence and the number
determined by it.

\item[5.] State fully what is meant by ``a limit of a sequence''
both for increasing and decreasing sequences.

\item[6.] Given two incommensurable segments $AB$ and $CD$.
Lay off on the line $AB$ a \emph{decreasing} sequence of segments,
each of which is commensurable with $CD$, such that the limit
of the sequence is the segment~$AB$.

\item[7.] If $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ is an increasing sequence defining the
number~$4$, prove that $3a_1$, $3a_2$, $3a_3$, $\dotsc$ defines the number
$3 × 4 = 12$.

\item[8.] If $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, and $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ are increasing sequences
defining the numbers $3$ and~$5$, show that the sequence $a_1b_1$,
$a_2b_2$, $a_3b_3$, $\dotsc$ defines the number~$15$.

\item[9.] Describe in more detail the meaning of the ratio of two
incommensurable arcs as indicated in §~\Sref{425}. Show that this
ratio is independent of the sequence of units of measurement
used, so long as the limit of this sequence is zero.

\item[10.] Treat the ratio of two incommensurable angles in a
manner similar to the treatment of arcs in the preceding
exercise.

\end{Itemize}
chapters.text_markdown:
It is often useful to think of a geometric figure as *varying* in size and shape.
*E.g.*, if a rectangle has a fixed base, say $10$ inches long, but an altitude which varies from $3$ inches to $5$ inches, then the area varies from $3 \cdot 10 = 30$ to $5 \cdot 10 = 50$ square inches. We may even think of the altitude as starting at zero inches and increasing, in which case the area starts at zero and increases continuously.
The altitude which we think of as varying at our pleasure is called the *independent variable*, while the area, being dependent upon the altitude, is called the *dependent variable*. The dependent variable is sometimes called a *function* of the independent variable, meaning that the two are connected by a definite relation such that, for any definite value of the independent variable, the dependent variable also has a definite value.
Thus, in the formula for the area of a rectangle, $a = bh$, if $b$ is fixed and $h$ varies, then $a$ is a function of $h$, since for every value of $h$ there is determined a definite value of $a$.
If a regular polygon is inscribed in a circle of fixed radius, and if the number of sides of the polygon be continually increased, for instance by repeatedly doubling the number, then the apothem, perimeter, and area are all variables depending upon the number of sides. That is, each of these is a function of the number of sides. Now the greater the number of sides the more nearly does the apothem equal the radius in length. Indeed, it is evident that the difference between the apothem and the radius will ultimately become less than any fixed number, however small. Hence we say that the apothem *approaches the radius as a limit* as the number of sides increases indefinitely. Similarly the perimeters of the polygons may be made as nearly equal to the circumference as we please by making the number of sides sufficiently great. Hence we may define the circumference of a circle as the *limit of the perimeter* of a regular inscribed polygon as the number of sides increases indefinitely. The circumference of a circle may also be defined as the limit of the perimeter of a circumscribed polygon as the number of sides is increased indefinitely. Likewise we may define the area of a circle as the *limit of the area* of the inscribed or the circumscribed polygon as the number of sides is increased indefinitely. The notion of a limit may be used to define the length of a line-segment which is incommensurable with a given unit segment.
Thus, the diagonal $d$ of a square whose side is unity is $d = \sqrt{2}$. Hence $d$ may be defined as the *limit of the variable line-segment* whose successive lengths are $1$, $1.4$, $1.41$, $1.414$, $\dotsc$.
In like manner, the length of any line-segment, whether commensurable or incommensurable with the unit segment, may be defined in terms of a limit.
Thus, if a variable segment is increased by successively adding to it one half the length previously added, then the segment will approach a limit. If the initial length is $1$, and if the successive additions are $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{1}{4}$, $\tfrac{1}{8}$, $\tfrac{1}{16}$, $\tfrac{1}{32}$, etc., then the successive lengths are $1$, $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{3}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{7}{8}$, $1 \tfrac{15}{16}$, $1 \tfrac{31}{32}$, etc. Evidently this segment approaches the limit $2$. Hence $2$ may be defined as the limit of the variable segment whose successive lengths are $1$, $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{3}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{7}{8}$, etc., as the number of successive additions is increased indefinitely.
The idea of a functional relation between variables and the idea of a limit, as illustrated above, are two of the most important concepts in all mathematics. A quantity which remains fixed in value throughout a discussion is called a *constant*.
*E.g.*, the base of the rectangle mentioned in §  is a constant.
A quantity which continuously changes in value, or which takes on a succession of different values, is called a *variable*.
*E.g.*, the altitude and the area mentioned in §  are variables.
If a variable may be made to approach a certain constant quantity in such a way that the difference between the constant and the variable becomes and remains less than any assignable value, however small, then the constant is called the *limit of the variable*.
*E.g.*, the fixed circumference of the circle is the limit of the variable perimeters of the polygons mentioned in § .
Find the limit of a variable line-segment whose initial length is $6$ inches, and which varies by successive increments each equal to one half the preceding, the first increment being $2$ inches. Construct a right triangle whose sides are $1$ and $2$. By approximating a square root, find five successive lengths of a segment which approaches the length of the hypotenuse as a limit. If one tangent to a circle is fixed and another is made to move so that their intersection point approaches the circle, what is the limiting position of the moving tangent? What is the limit of the measure of the angle formed by these tangents? The arc $AB$ of $74$° is the greater of the two arcs intercepted between two secants meeting at $C$ outside the circle. The points $A$ and $B$ remain fixed while $C$ moves up to the circle. What angle is the limit of the variable angle formed by the varying secants? What is the limit of the measure of this angle? If in the preceding the secants meet within the circle, what is the limit of their angle and also of the measure of this angle as the intersection point moves up to the center of the circle?
We have seen that there are segments which are *incommensurable*; that is, which have no common unit of measure,---for instance, the side and the diagonal of a square. For *practical purposes* the lengths of such segments are approximated to any desired degree of accuracy, and their ratios are understood to be the ratios of these approximate numerical measures. But for *theoretical purposes* it is important to consider these incommensurable cases further; just as in algebra we not only *approximate* such roots as $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$, $\sqrt{5}$, etc., but we also deal with these surds as *exact* numbers.
Instances of this kind occur in such operations as $$(\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{2})(\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}) = 3 - 2 = 1.$$
While the length of the diagonal of a unit square cannot be expressed as an integer or as a rational fraction, that is, as the quotient of two integers, we nevertheless think of such a segment as having a *definite length*, or what is the same thing, a *definite ratio* with the unit segment forming the side of the square. We now fix our attention on the *incommensurable ratios themselves*, and the method of determining them, rather than on the *process of approach* and the practical computation based on it. In general, the ratio between any two incommensurable geometric magnitudes of the same kind may be represented by what is called an *irrational number*; that is, a number which is *neither an integer nor a quotient of two integers*. Examples of irrational numbers are the surds, such as $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt[3]{5}$, etc., and the number $\pi$. The following is a method for determining any number, whether rational or irrational. For simplicity it is applied first to the integer $1$. Throughout this discussion the expressions "point on a line" and "number" will be used interchangeably.
r2.25in
On a straight line mark a certain point $0$ (zero), and one unit to the right of it mark another point $1$. Also lay off points such that their distances from $0$ are $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$, $\tfrac{7}{8}$, $\tfrac{15}{16}$, $\dotsc$. If this sequence of points is carried ever so far, it will never reach the point $1$. If, however, we select a point to the left of $1$, no matter how near to it, we may always go far enough along this sequence to reach points between this point and $1$. That is, $1$ is the limit of the terms of this sequence. See § .
The point $1$ has two definite relations to this sequence: (a) *Every point of the sequence is to the left of $1$*. (b) *For any fixed point to the left of $1$ there are points of the sequence between it and $1$*. We see that $1$ is the *only* point on the whole line such that both (a) and (b) are true of it. For every point to the right of $1$ (a) is true, but (b) is not. For every point to the left of $1$ (b) is true, but (a) is not. It follows therefore that, while the points of the sequence merely *approach* the point $1$ as a limit, the sequence, *taken as a whole, serves to distinguish that point from all other points on the line*.
In the above sequence, the terms continually *increase*. The number $1$ may be determined equally well by a *decreasing* sequence. For instance, the sequence $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{8}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{16}$, $\dotsc$ has the following properties which distinguish the point $1$ from all other points on the line.
(a) *Every point of the sequence is to the right of $1$*. (b) *For any fixed point to the right of $1$ there are points of the sequence between it and $1$*. An endless sequence of either kind just described is called an *infinite sequence*. Not every infinite sequence serves to single out a definite point in the manner shown above. Thus the sequence $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $\dotsc$ fails to do so, because its terms grow large beyond all bound. Such sequences are said to be *unbounded*, while the sequences $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$, $\tfrac{7}{8}$, $\dotsc$ and $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{8}$, $\dotsc$ are *bounded*. Again, the sequence $1$, $2$, $1$, $2$, $1$, $2$, $\dotsc$ fails to single out a definite point. This sequence is said to be *oscillating*, since its terms increase, then decrease, then increase, etc., while $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$, $\tfrac{7}{8}$, $\dotsc$ and $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{8}$, $\dotsc$ are *non-oscillating*. The number $1$ is said to be the *least upper bound* of the sequence $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$, $\tfrac{7}{8}$, $\dotsc$. That is, $1$ is the *smallest number* beyond which the sequence does not go. $1$ is also said to be the *limit of the sequence*. See § . Similarly, $1$ is the *greatest lower bound* or the *limit* of the sequence $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{1}{8}$, $\dotsc$; that is, the *greatest number* such that the sequence contains no number less than it. In the manner described above any integer may be determined by an increasing or a decreasing infinite sequence.
*E.g.*, the number $2$ is the limit of the increasing sequence $1$, $1 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $1 \tfrac{3}{4}$, $1 \tfrac{7}{8}$, $1 \tfrac{15}{16}$, $\dotsc$, or of the decreasing sequence $2 \tfrac{1}{2}$, $2 \tfrac{1}{4}$, $2 \tfrac{1}{8}$, $2 \tfrac{1}{16}$, $\dotsc$.
Two different sequences, both increasing or both decreasing, may also define the same number.
*E.g.*, each of the increasing sequences $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$, $\tfrac{7}{8}$, $\tfrac{15}{16}$, $\dotsc$ and $\tfrac{2}{3}$, $\tfrac{4}{5}$, $\tfrac{6}{7}$, $\tfrac{8}{9}$, $\dotsc$ determines the number $1$. We notice, however, that no matter what definite number we select in either of these sequences, there is a number in the other greater than it; that is, neither sequence contains a number greater than every number in the other. See § .
It is apparent that any number may be defined as the limit of a sequence, and we shall assume the converse, namely, that any bounded increasing or decreasing sequence has a limit.
418. We now assume that: *Every bounded increasing sequence has a least upper bound, and every bounded decreasing sequence has a greatest lower bound*.
This axiom may also be stated: *Every bounded increasing or decreasing sequence has a limit*. This axiom simply means that every such sequence singles out a definite number, rational or irrational, in the manner discussed on page .
Thus, if we attempt to approximate the square root of $2$, we obtain a sequence, $1$, $1.4$, $1.41$, $1.414$, $1.4142$, $\dotsc$, having for its limit a *definite number* represented by $\sqrt{2}$, which corresponds to the length of the diagonal of a square whose side is unity. Again, if we attempt to approximate the value of $\pi$, we obtain a sequence $3$, $3.1$, $3.14$, $3.141$, $3.1415$, $\dotsc$, having for its limit the definite number represented by $\pi$, which is the ratio of the circumference to the diameter of a circle.
419.I. Two bounded sequences have the same limit if they are equal term by term.
: If the sequences are $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ and $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$, and if $a_1 = b_1$, $a_2 = b_2$, $a_3 = b_3$, $\dotsc$, then they are one and the same sequence and hence have the same limit by § .
**Historical Note**.The rigorous treatment of limits has been developed during the last fifty years. The foundation on which it rests is the theory of irrational numbers, which itself was placed on a firm basis in the early seventies. The Greeks dealt with the incommensurable cases in an interesting manner. Thus, to prove that two incommensurable ratios are equal they showed that neither can be less than the other. However, they failed to make explicit definitions of incommensurables and they did not explicitly state the fundamental axiom of §  or its equivalent. Their treatment would be complete and rigorous if supplemented by the proper definitions and axioms.
420.II. Two increasing bounded sequences have the same limit if neither sequence contains a number greater than every number of the other.
Let $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ and $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ denote two infinite sequences with limits $a$ and $b$, such that no term of the first sequence is greater than every term of the second, and no term of the second is greater than every term of the first. *To prove that $a = b$*. : Suppose that $a$ is not equal to $b$ but is less than $b$. Then there must be numbers of the sequence $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ greater than $a$, since by §  there are numbers $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, greater than any fixed number whatever which is less than $b$. This contradicts the hypothesis of the theorem, and hence $a$ cannot be less than $b$. In like manner we show that $b$ is not less than $a$. Hence $a = b$. See § .
421.III. Two decreasing bounded sequences have the same limit if neither sequence contains a number less than every number of the other.
: The proof is exactly similar to that of Theorem II.
Show that the sequences $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$, $\tfrac{7}{8}$, $\dotsc$ and $\tfrac{2}{3}$, $\tfrac{4}{5}$, $\tfrac{6}{7}$, $\dotsc$ have the same limits. Show that the sequences $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{1}{4}$, $\tfrac{1}{8}$, $\dotsc$ and $\tfrac{1}{3}$, $\tfrac{1}{5}$, $\tfrac{1}{7}$, $\dotsc$ have the same limits.
The applications of the theory of limits to geometry consist chiefly in showing that two numbers are equal because they are the limits of the same sequence, or of sequences having the property stated in the theorem of §  or of § .
422. On a given segment $AB$ to lay off a sequence of points $B_1$, $B_2$, $B_3$, $\dotsc$, of which $B$ is the limit, such that each of the segments $AB_1$, $AB_2$, $AB_3$, $\dotsc$ is commensurable with a given segment $CD$.
*Solution*:Using $m_1$, an exact divisor of $CD$, as a unit of measure, lay off on $AB$ a segment $AB_1$, an exact multiple of $m_1$, such that the remainder $B_1B$ is less than $m_1$. Then $CD$ and $AB_1$ are commensurable. Using a unit $m_2$, likewise a divisor of $CD$, and less than $B_1B$, lay off $AB_2$ such that $B_2B$ is less than $m_2$. Then $AB_2 > AB_1$, and $CD$ and $AB_2$ are commensurable. Continuing in this manner, using as units of measure segments $m_3$, $m_4$, $\dotsc$ each an exact divisor of $CD$ and each less than $B_2B$, $B_3B$, $\dotsc$ respectively, we obtain a sequence of segments $AB_1$, $AB_2$, $AB_3$, $\dotsc$, each greater than the preceding and each commensurable with $CD$. If the units $m_1$, $m_2$, $m_3$, $\dotsc$ are so selected that they approach zero as a limit, it follows that $B$ is the limit point of the sequence $B_1$, $B_2$, $B_3$, $\dotsc$. If a different sequence of divisors of $CD$, as $m_1'$, $m_2'$, $m_3'$, $\dotsc$, is used, we obtain a sequence of points $B_1'$, $B_2'$, $B_3'$, $\dotsc$, likewise satisfying the conditions of the problem. Any two such sequences of points $B_1$, $B_2$, $B_3$, $\dotsc$ and $B_1'$, $B_2'$, $B_3'$, $\dotsc$ determined as above, are both *increasing* and each is such that *no* point of it is to the right of *every* point of the other. Hence, by §  any two such sequences have the same limit point $B$. If $B_1$, $B_2$, $B_3$, $\dotsc$ is a sequence of points on the segment $AB$ having the limit $B$, then the segment $AB$ is said to *be the limit of the sequence of segments* $AB_1$, $AB_2$, $AB_3$, $\dotsc$. The ratio of two incommensurable segments has not been explicitly defined, but this may now be done in terms of the *limit of a sequence*. Consider two incommensurable segments $AB$ and $CD$. Let $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ be the lengths of segments each commensurable with $CD$, forming a sequence whose limit is the segment $AB$, and let $b$ be the length of the segment $CD$. Then $\dfrac{a_1}{b}$, $\dfrac{a_2}{b}$, $\dfrac{a_3}{b}$, $\dotsc$ is an increasing bounded sequence having a limit which we call $R$. If $a_1'$, $a_2'$, $a_3'$, $\dotsc$ are the lengths of segments forming any other sequence whose limit is $AB$, the sequence $\dfrac{a_1'}{b}$, $\dfrac{a_2'}{b}$, $\dfrac{a_3'}{b}$, $\dotsc$ is another increasing bounded sequence with limit $R'$. By §  we now know that $R = R'$. This number $R$ is defined as *the ratio of the incommensurable segments* $AB$ and $CD$. The considerations of §§ , , apply to two arcs of equal circles.
Thus, in the figure, the ratio of the two incommensurable arcs $AB$ and $CD$ is the limit of the sequence $\dfrac{AB_1}{CD}$, $\dfrac{AB_2}{CD}$, $\dfrac{AB_3}{CD}$, $\dotsc$, and the ratio of the incommensurable angles $AOB$ and $COD$ is the limit of the sequence $\dfrac{\angle AOB_1}{\angle COD}$, $\dfrac{\angle AOB_2}{\angle COD}$, $\dfrac{\angle AOB_3}{\angle COD}$, $\dotsc$.
426.IV. A line parallel to the base of a triangle, and meeting the other two sides, divides them in the same ratio.
To prove that $\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{AE}{AC}$. : Consider the case when $AD$ and $AB$ are incommensurable. Let $D_1$, $D_2$, $D_3$, $\dotsc$ be a sequence of points on $AB$ whose limit is $D$. Through these points draw parallels to $BC$, meeting $AC$ in $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$, $\dotsc$.
Then $E$ is the limit of the sequence of points $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$, $\dotsc$. For suppose it is not, and that there is a point $K$ on $AE$ such that there is no point of $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$, $\dotsc$ between $K$ and $E$. Draw a line parallel to $BC$ through $K$, meeting $AB$ in $H$. But there are points of the sequence $D_1$, $D_2$, $D_3$, *between* $H$ and $D$, and hence there must be points of the sequence $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$, $\dotsc$ between $K$ and $E$, which shows that $E$ is the limit of the sequence $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$, $\dotsc$. Then the sequence (1) $\dfrac{AD_1}{AB}$, $\dfrac{AD_2}{AB}$, $\dfrac{AD_3}{AB}$, $\dotsc$ has a limit $R$ which, by definition, is the ratio of the segments $AD$ and $AB$. §  Similarly, the sequence (2) $\dfrac{AE_1}{AC}$, $\dfrac{AE_2}{AC}$, $\dfrac{AE_3}{AC}$, $\dotsc$ has a limit $R'$ which is the ratio of $AE$ to $AC$. Now $\dfrac{AD_1}{AB} = \dfrac{AE_1}{AC}$, $\dfrac{AD_2}{AB} = \dfrac{AE_2}{AC}$, $\dfrac{AD_3}{AB} = \dfrac{AE_3}{AC}$, $\dotsc$ § 321, P. G. Hence, the two sequences, (1) and (2), are identical and have the same limit (§ ). Hence $R = R'$.
427.V. In the same circle or in equal circles the ratio of two central angles is the same as the ratio of their intercepted arcs.
: In case the arcs are commensurable the proof is obvious. For, in that case, the common measure of the arcs divides each into a number of equal parts, say $m$ and $n$ respectively, and these arcs subtend the same number of equal angles at the center (§ , Plane Geometry.) Hence the ratio of the arcs is $m : n$ and the ratio of the angles is also $m : n$. If the arcs $AB$ and $CD$ are not commensurable, let $AB_1$, $AB_2$, $AB_3$, $\dotsc$ be a sequence of arcs whose limit is $AB$, each arc being commensurable with the arc $CD$. Then the sequence $\dfrac{AB_1}{CD}$, $\dfrac{AB_2}{CD}$, $\dfrac{AB_3}{CD}$, $\dotsc$ has a limit $R = \dfrac{AB}{CD}$. Similarly the sequence $\dfrac{\angle AOB_1}{\angle COD}$, $\dfrac{\angle AOB_2}{\angle COD}$, $\dfrac{\angle AOB_3}{\angle COD}$, $\dotsc$ has a limit $R' = \dfrac{\angle AOB}{\angle COD}$. But $\dfrac{AB_1}{CD} = \dfrac{\angle AOB_1}{\angle COD}$, $\dfrac{AB_2}{CD} = \dfrac{\angle AOB_2}{\angle COD}$, $\dotsc$, as shown above for the commensurable case. Hence, these two sequences are identical and have the same limit (§ ). Therefore it follows that $R = R'$.
*Note*.---The student should note the successive steps in the proofs of §§ , : (a) Definitions of the incommensurable ratios by means of infinite sequences; (b) Proof that these sequences are identical; (c) Conclusion that the limiting ratios are equal.
If $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ is a sequence with limit $a$, then $ka_1$, $ka_2$, $ka_3$, $\dotsc$ is a sequence whose limit is *defined* as $ka$ where $k$ is any number. If $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ and $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ are two sequences with limits $a$ and $b$ respectively, then $a_1b_1$, $a_2b_2$, $a_3b_3$, $\dotsc$ is a sequence whose limit is *defined* as $ab$. Similarly if $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$, $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ and $c_1$, $c_2$, $c_3$, $\dotsc$ are sequences with limits $a$, $b$, $c$, then $abc$ is defined as the limit of the sequence $a_1b_1c_1$, $a_2b_2c_2$, $a_3b_3c_3$, $\dotsc$. For a complete treatment it would be necessary to show that these definitions of multiplication of irrational numbers are consistent with the rest of arithmetic and also that these new sequences are such as to determine definite limits. This is possible but is beyond the scope of this book. If the sides of a rectangle are incommensurable with the unit segment, we *define its area* as follows: Let $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ be a sequence of rational numbers whose limit is the altitude $a$; and let $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ be a sequence whose limit is the base $b$. Then the area of the rectangle is the limit of the sequence $a_1b_1$, $a_2b_2$, $a_3b_3$, $\dotsc$.
But by definition the limit of $a_1b_1$, $a_2b_2$, $a_3b_3$, $\dotsc$ is the product $ab$. Hence we have the theorem:
430.VI. The area of a rectangle is the product of its base and altitude.
In a circle inscribe a sequence $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, $\dotsc$ of regular polygons, each having twice the number of sides of the one preceding it.
Let the perimeters of these polygons be $p_1$, $p_2$, $p_3$, $\dotsc$ and their areas $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $\dotsc$. Then the length $c$ of the circle is defined to be the limit of the sequence $p_1$, $p_2$, $p_3$, $\dotsc$ and its area $A$ is defined to be the limit of $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $\dotsc$. The sequence of polygons thus inscribed is called an *approximating sequence of polygons*.
That these sequences are *increasing* and *bounded* is obvious from the figure.
432.VII. The lengths of two circles are in the same ratio as their radii, and their areas are in the same ratio as the squares of their radii.
: Let the radii of the two circles be $r$ and $r'$. Denote the ratio $r':r$ by $k$. Then $r' = kr$. Inscribe in one circle an approximating sequence of polygons with perimeters $p_1$, $p_2$, $p_3$, $\dotsc$ and areas $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $\dotsc$. In the other circle inscribe a sequence of similar polygons. By §§ 476, 477 (Plane Geometry), the perimeters of the latter are $kp_1$, $kp_2$, $kp_3$, $\dotsc$ and their areas are $k^2A_1$, $k^2A_2$, $k^2A_3$, $\dotsc$. By § , if the limit of $p_1$, $p_2$, $p_3$, $\dotsc$ is $c$ and the limit of $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $\dotsc$ is $A$, then the limits of $kp_1$, $kp_2$, $kp_3$, $\dotsc$, and $k^2A_1$, $k^2A_2$, $k^2A_3$, $\dotsc$ are $kc$ and $k^2A$, respectively. That is, the ratio of the lengths of the circles is $\dfrac{kc}{c} = k= \dfrac{r'}{r}$ and the ratio of their areas is $\dfrac{k^2A}{A} = k^2 = \dfrac{r'^2}{r^2}$. The areas of curved surfaces, the volumes of cones, cylinders, and spheres, and even of rectangular solids involve *incommensurable quantities*. We have already treated these cases informally and have devised means for computing them *approximately*. We now give a formal treatment for logical completeness. If the three concurrent edges $a$, $b$, $c$ of a rectangular parallelopiped are incommensurable with the unit segment, the volume inclosed is defined as follows: Let $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ be a sequence of rational numbers whose limit is the side $a$. Let $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ and $c_1$, $c_2$, $c_3$, $\dotsc$ be similar sequences whose limits are respectively the dimensions $b$ and $c$.
Then the volume is the limit of the sequence $a_1b_1c_1$, $a_2b_2c_2$, $a_3b_3c_3$, $\dotsc$. But the limit of this sequence is by definition the product of the limits of the three sequences $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$, $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$, $c_1$, $c_2$, $c_3$, $\dotsc$, or $abc$.
Hence, we have the theorem:
435.VIII. The volume of a rectangular parallelopiped is equal to the product of its three concurrent edges.
Give in decimals four terms of a sequence which approximates the volume of a rectangular parallelopiped whose dimensions are $2$, $4$, $\sqrt{5}$. Give in decimals four terms of a sequence which approximates the circumference of a circle whose radius is $10$ in.; also of a sequence which approximates the area.
In a triangular pyramid inscribe a set of prisms in a manner similar to that shown in the figure of § . Call $V_1$ the sum of the volumes of these inscribed prisms. Using as altitudes one half the altitudes of the first set of prisms, inscribe a second set the sum of whose volumes is $V_2$. Continuing in this manner, we obtain a sequence of sets of prisms with volumes $V_1$, $V_2$, $V_3$, $\dotsc$. The limit $V$ of this sequence we define as **the volume of the pyramid**.
Circumscribed prisms may also be used for defining the volume of a pyramid, in which, case we get a *decreasing* sequence of volumes $U_1$, $U_2$, $U_3$, $\dotsc$, with limit $U$. That $U = V$ follows from the fact that the sum of the volumes of the circumscribed prisms exceeds that of the inscribed prisms by the volume of the lowest circumscribed prism, and this may be made as small as we please.
437.IX. Two pyramids with the same altitudes and equivalent bases have equal volumes.
: Call a sequence of inscribed prisms in one pyramid $V_1$, $V_2$, $V_3$, $\dotsc$, and in the other $V'_1$, $V'_2$, $V'_3$, $\dotsc$. Since corresponding sets of these prisms have equal volumes (§ ), that is, $V_1 = V'_1$, $V_2 = V'_2$, $V_3 = V'_3$, $\dotsc$, the theorem follows from § . These limits $p$ and $A$ we now define as **the perimeter and the area respectively of the curve**. Given any cylinder with a convex right cross-section and an element $e$. In this cross-section inscribe a sequence $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, $\dotsc$ of polygons, as in § , with perimeters $p_1$, $p_2$, $p_3$, $\dotsc$ and areas $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $\dotsc$, thus defining the perimeter $p$ and the area $A$ of the cross-section. Consider a set of prisms inscribed in this cylinder, of which $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, $\dotsc$ are right cross-sections. Then the areas and the volumes of these prisms are respectively $p_1e$, $p_2e$, $p_3e$, $\dotsc$ and $A_1e$, $A_2e$, $A_3e$, $\dotsc$. **The lateral area and the volume of the cylinder are now defined as the limits of these sequences**.But by §  these limits are equal respectively to $pe$ and $Ae$. 440.X. The lateral area of a cylinder is the product of an element, and the perimeter of a right section and its volume is the product of an element and the area of a right section.
