(2) $\text{Vol.\ } CBE = \pi CB \cdot \overline{BE}^2 = \pi CB(r^2 - \overline{OB}^2)$, since\ $\overline{BE}^2 = r^2 - \overline{OB}^2$. But $OB = O'B'$ and $CB = C'B'$. Hence, $\text{Vol.\ } CBE = \pi C'B'(r^2 - \overline{O'B'}^2)$. Hence, $\text{Vol.\ } CBE = \text{Vol.\ } C'B'E' - \text{Vol.\ } C'B'K$. Similarly we show that $$\text{Vol.\ } OCD = \text{Vol.\ } O'C'D' - \text{Vol.\ } O'C'H.$$ Hence, $V_1 = V'_1$. In like manner $V_2 = V'_2$, $V_3 = V'_3$, $\dotsc$. Hence, $V = V'$, since they are the limits of the same sequences. But the volume of the cylinder $O'A'M$ is $\pi r^3$ and of the cone whose volume was subtracted, $\tfrac{1}{3} \pi r^3$. That is, the volume of $F$ is $\tfrac{2}{3} \pi r^3$, and hence that of the hemisphere is $\tfrac{2}{3} \pi r^3$. Hence, we have the theorem:
443.XI. The volume of the sphere is $\tfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3$.
Note that the above proof consists essentially in showing that the area of the circle $BE$ is equal to that of the ring between the circles $B'E'$ and $B'K$, and that the area of the circle $CD$ is equal to that of the ring between $C'D'$ and $C'H$ and so on. Indeed, this theorem and also that of §  are special cases of what is known as **Cavalieri's Theorem**.
444.XII. If two solid figures are regarded as resting on the same plane $b$, and if in every plane parallel to $b$ the sections of the two figures have equal areas, the figures have equal volumes.
The proof of this general theorem is more difficult than any thus far given, inasmuch as it involves sequences which *oscillate*; that is, which are neither constantly increasing nor constantly decreasing. About a sphere of radius $r$ construct a sequence of circumscribed polyhedrons such that the largest face in each polyhedron becomes as small as we please when we proceed along the sequence. Let $s_1$, $s_2$, $s_3$, $\dotsc$ be the total surfaces of these polyhedrons. This forms a decreasing sequence with limit $S$ which we define as **the surface of the sphere**. The volumes of these polyhedrons will be $\tfrac{1}{3}rs_1$, $\tfrac{1}{3}rs_2$, $\tfrac{1}{3}rs_3$, $\dotsc$. Then the volume $V$ of the sphere is defined[^2] as **the limit of this sequence of volumes**. Hence, by § , $V = \tfrac{1}{3}rS$. But by § , $V = \tfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3$. $S = \tfrac{3}{r} \cdot \tfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 = 4 \pi r^2$. Hence, we have the theorem:
446.XIII. The area of the sphere is $4 \pi r^2$.
In addition to those which are found in the text give other examples of infinite sequences which do not determine definite numbers. Give two increasing sequences which determine the number $3$. Show that the theorem of §  applies and proves that these sequences determine the same number. Give two decreasing sequences each of which determines the number $5$. Apply §  to show that these sequences determine the same number. State fully the relation between a bounded increasing sequence and the number determined by it. State also the relations between a bounded decreasing sequence and the number determined by it. State fully what is meant by "a limit of a sequence" both for increasing and decreasing sequences. Given two incommensurable segments $AB$ and $CD$. Lay off on the line $AB$ a *decreasing* sequence of segments, each of which is commensurable with $CD$, such that the limit of the sequence is the segment $AB$. If $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\dotsc$ is an increasing sequence defining the number $4$, prove that $3a_1$, $3a_2$, $3a_3$, $\dotsc$ defines the number $3 × 4 = 12$. If $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, and $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, $\dotsc$ are increasing sequences defining the numbers $3$ and $5$, show that the sequence $a_1b_1$, $a_2b_2$, $a_3b_3$, $\dotsc$ defines the number $15$. Describe in more detail the meaning of the ratio of two incommensurable arcs as indicated in § . Show that this ratio is independent of the sequence of units of measurement used, so long as the limit of this sequence is zero. Treat the ratio of two incommensurable angles in a manner similar to the treatment of arcs in the preceding exercise.
[^1]: This theorem was discovered by Cavalieri. See [Frontispiece](#page:Cavalieri). [^2]: This definition can be shown to be consistent with that of § .
chapters.name: Slaught & Lennes 1919, ch. Appendix III: VARIABLES. LIMITS

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: In plane geometry each figure is restricted so that all of its parts lie in the same plane. Such figures are called \emph{two-dimensional figures}.
excerpts.markdown: In plane geometry each figure is restricted so that all of its parts lie in the same plane. Such figures are called *two-dimensional figures*.
excerpts.why: Gives the learner the defining restriction that separates plane figures from solid ones.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: A figure, all parts of which lie in one straight line, is a \emph{one-dimensional figure}, while a point is of zero dimensions.
excerpts.markdown: A figure, all parts of which lie in one straight line, is a *one-dimensional figure*, while a point is of zero dimensions.
excerpts.why: Places the line and the point on the same ladder of dimensions as plane and solid figures.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: In plane geometry, two lines which do not meet are parallel, while in solid geometry, two lines which do not meet need not be parallel. That is, they may not be in the same plane. Lines which are not parallel and do not meet are called \emph{skew} lines.
excerpts.markdown: In plane geometry, two lines which do not meet are parallel, while in solid geometry, two lines which do not meet need not be parallel. That is, they may not be in the same plane. Lines which are not parallel and do not meet are called *skew* lines.
excerpts.why: Shows a learner why a fact that is true in the plane fails in space, and names the new case.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: In plane geometry, ``the locus of all points at a given distance from a given point'' is a circle, while in solid geometry this locus is a sphere.
excerpts.markdown: In plane geometry, “the locus of all points at a given distance from a given point” is a circle, while in solid geometry this locus is a sphere.
excerpts.why: A short contrast that lets a learner see how the same definition of locus changes its shape when a dimension is added.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: If all parts of the figure are not required to lie in one plane, the theorem just quoted is far from true.
excerpts.markdown: If all parts of the figure are not required to lie in one plane, the theorem just quoted is far from true.
excerpts.why: Warns the learner that a plane theorem cannot be carried into space without checking its hypothesis.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: A plane is designated by a single letter in it, by two letters at opposite corners of the parallelogram representing it, or by any three letters in it but not in the same straight line.
excerpts.markdown: A plane is designated by a single letter in it, by two letters at opposite corners of the parallelogram representing it, or by any three letters in it but not in the same straight line.
excerpts.why: Gives the three standard ways to name a plane, which the learner will use throughout the book.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The area of a circle is one half the circumference times the radius, or in symbols:
excerpts.markdown: The area of a circle is one half the circumference times the radius, or in symbols:
excerpts.why: Presents the area of a circle as a consequence of circumference and radius, a link a learner can check against the formula that follows.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Through a point not on a given line only one straight line can be drawn parallel to that line.
excerpts.markdown: Through a point not on a given line only one straight line can be drawn parallel to that line.
excerpts.why: States the parallel postulate that plane geometry rests on, the premise the space results later qualify.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: If a line or a plane contains a point, the point is said to be \emph{on} the line or \emph{in} the plane and the line or plane is said to pass \emph{through} the point.
excerpts.markdown: If a line or a plane contains a point, the point is said to be *on* the line or *in* the plane and the line or plane is said to pass *through* the point.
excerpts.why: It fixes the basic vocabulary of 'on', 'in' and 'through' that every later figure relies on.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: While two points determine a straight line it is obvious that two points do not determine a plane.
excerpts.markdown: While two points determine a straight line it is obvious that two points do not determine a plane.
excerpts.why: It shows a learner why three points, not two, are needed to fix a plane.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: We, therefore, say that three non-collinear points determine a plane, while any number of collinear points fail to determine a plane.
excerpts.markdown: We, therefore, say that three non-collinear points determine a plane, while any number of collinear points fail to determine a plane.
excerpts.why: It states the rule for when points fix a plane, in the form a student can apply directly.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: In the figure, $PA$ is perpendicular to the plane~$M$ and $QA$ is oblique to it.
excerpts.markdown: In the figure, $PA$ is perpendicular to the plane $M$ and $QA$ is oblique to it.
excerpts.why: It sets a perpendicular line beside an oblique one from the same foot, so the contrast is visible.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The perpendicular is the shortest distance from a point to a plane.
excerpts.markdown: The perpendicular is the shortest distance from a point to a plane.
excerpts.why: It explains why the distance from a point to a plane is measured along the perpendicular.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Note that the four vertices of a quadrilateral in space do not necessarily all lie in the same plane.
excerpts.markdown: Note that the four vertices of a quadrilateral in space do not necessarily all lie in the same plane.
excerpts.why: It warns learners not to assume that four points in space are coplanar.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Any line, as $l_1$, in either of two parallel planes, $M$ and $N$, is parallel to the other plane.
excerpts.markdown: Any line, as $l_1$, in either of two parallel planes, $M$ and $N$, is parallel to the other plane.
excerpts.why: It links parallel planes to lines parallel to a plane, which is how the parallel theorems are later used.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: If two straight lines are cut by three parallel planes, the intercepted segments on one line are proportional to the corresponding segments on the other.
excerpts.markdown: If two straight lines are cut by three parallel planes, the intercepted segments on one line are proportional to the corresponding segments on the other.
excerpts.why: States the central result of the section in a form a learner can apply to a slanting rod cut by parallel shelves.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Two half-planes meeting in a common edge form a \emph{dihedral angle}.
excerpts.markdown: Two half-planes meeting in a common edge form a *dihedral angle*.
excerpts.why: Gives the defining sentence of a dihedral angle, the solid-geometry analogue of a plane angle.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: angle may be thought of as \emph{generated} by the rotation of a half-plane about its edge. The magnitude of the angle depends solely upon the \emph{amount of rotation}.
excerpts.markdown: angle may be thought of as *generated* by the rotation of a half-plane about its edge. The magnitude of the angle depends solely upon the *amount of rotation*.
excerpts.why: A concrete picture of a dihedral angle as a turning half-plane, which makes its size easy to grasp.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: point on a plane is the foot of the perpendicular from the point to the plane.
excerpts.markdown: point on a plane is the foot of the perpendicular from the point to the plane.
excerpts.why: Defines the projection of a point, the basis for every later projection argument in the chapter.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The acute angle formed by a straight line with its own projection on a plane is the least angle which it makes with any line in that plane.
excerpts.markdown: The acute angle formed by a straight line with its own projection on a plane is the least angle which it makes with any line in that plane.
excerpts.why: A vivid minimum property that explains why the angle between a line and a plane is defined through its projection.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The trihedral angles $O$ and $O'$ cannot be made to coincide, even though their corresponding parts are equal. This can be illustrated by attempting to put a left glove on the right hand.
excerpts.markdown: The trihedral angles $O$ and $O'$ cannot be made to coincide, even though their corresponding parts are equal. This can be illustrated by attempting to put a left glove on the right hand.
excerpts.why: The glove image makes the idea of mirror-image order of parts memorable for a learner.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Show that line-segments included between parallel planes and perpendicular to them are equal, and hence that parallel planes are everywhere equally distant.
excerpts.markdown: Show that line-segments included between parallel planes and perpendicular to them are equal, and hence that parallel planes are everywhere equally distant.
excerpts.why: A practical exercise that links parallel planes to the carpenter's task of placing two shelves level.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: A polyhedron is \emph{convex} if every section of it made by a plane is a convex polygon.
excerpts.markdown: A polyhedron is *convex* if every section of it made by a plane is a convex polygon.
excerpts.why: It gives the test a learner can apply to any solid: slice it with a plane and check whether every section is convex.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: These names are all derived from the Greek and refer to the number of faces.
excerpts.markdown: These names are all derived from the Greek and refer to the number of faces.
excerpts.why: It shows the learner that the names of the polyhedrons are a code: the Greek root gives the number of faces.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The faces, edges, and vertices taken together form the surface of the polyhedron.
excerpts.markdown: The faces, edges, and vertices taken together form the surface of the polyhedron.
excerpts.why: It pins down what the surface of a solid is, so learners can separate the boundary from the solid it encloses.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: From these propositions it follows that each of the polyhedral angles of a regular polyhedron may be formed by three, four, or five (but not six) equilateral triangles; by three (but not four) squares; or by three (but not four) regular pentagons.
excerpts.markdown: From these propositions it follows that each of the polyhedral angles of a regular polyhedron may be formed by three, four, or five (but not six) equilateral triangles; by three (but not four) squares; or by three (but not four) regular pentagons.
excerpts.why: It turns the two face-angle facts into the concrete list of which regular polygons can meet at a vertex, which is the core reason there are only five.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: \textit{The sum of the face angles of a polyhedral angle is less than~$360$°}.
excerpts.markdown: *The sum of the face angles of a polyhedral angle is less than $360$°*.
excerpts.why: It states the limit that stops a vertex from closing up flat, which the learner needs before testing any candidate polygon.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: At the center~$E$ of an equilateral triangle~$ABC$ erect a perpendicular to the plane of the triangle.
excerpts.markdown: At the center $E$ of an equilateral triangle $ABC$ erect a perpendicular to the plane of the triangle.
excerpts.why: It shows how a regular solid is built from one equilateral triangle by erecting a perpendicular at its centre, a step the learner can carry out with card and a ruler.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: \textit{Two polyhedrons have the same volume if they can be made to coincide, or if they can be divided into parts which can be made to coincide in pairs}.
excerpts.markdown: *Two polyhedrons have the same volume if they can be made to coincide, or if they can be divided into parts which can be made to coincide in pairs*.
excerpts.why: It states the principle that lets volumes of general prisms be found by cutting and rearranging solids, without new measurement.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Any prism, can be divided into triangular prisms by planes passing through one edge and each of the other non-adjacent edges.
excerpts.markdown: Any prism, can be divided into triangular prisms by planes passing through one edge and each of the other non-adjacent edges.
excerpts.why: This is the method for reducing any prism to triangular prisms, whose volume is already known.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: but no attempt has been made to \emph{measure the space occupied} by such a solid. For this purpose we consider first a rectangular parallelopiped.
excerpts.markdown: but no attempt has been made to *measure the space occupied* by such a solid. For this purpose we consider first a rectangular parallelopiped.
excerpts.why: It frames volume as a new question about the space a solid occupies, and says why the book starts with the simplest box.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Since the edge~$BE$ is $5$~units long, $5$ such tiers will exactly fill the space within the solid. That is, $5\cdot 3\cdot 4 = 60$ is the number of cubic units in the solid.
excerpts.markdown: Since the edge $BE$ is $5$ units long, $5$ such tiers will exactly fill the space within the solid. That is, $5\cdot 3\cdot 4 = 60$ is the number of cubic units in the solid.
excerpts.why: A small whole-number example shows, by counting layers of unit cubes, why volume is the product of the three edges.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: E.g.,~if the length is $5$~inches and the width is $\sqrt{3}$~inches, then the base cannot be exactly covered with equal cubes, however small.
excerpts.markdown: E.g., if the length is $5$ inches and the width is $\sqrt{3}$ inches, then the base cannot be exactly covered with equal cubes, however small.
excerpts.why: It shows learners that some lengths cannot be measured by any unit cube exactly, which is why the book uses approximation.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The form of statement in this theorem is the usual abbreviation for the more \emph{precise} form:
excerpts.markdown: The form of statement in this theorem is the usual abbreviation for the more *precise* form:
excerpts.why: It warns learners that the statement 'lateral area equals edge times perimeter' means the numerical measures of those lengths, a common source of confusion.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Indeed, in these cases approximate measurement only is possible, since no square unit exists in terms of which such areas can be \emph{exactly} measured.
excerpts.markdown: Indeed, in these cases approximate measurement only is possible, since no square unit exists in terms of which such areas can be *exactly* measured.
excerpts.why: It explains why curved surfaces need approximation, by contrast with plane figures, which can be measured exactly.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: \textit{A cylinder has a definite lateral area and a definite volume which may be approximated as nearly as we please by taking the lateral areas and the volumes of successive inscribed or circumscribed prisms}.
excerpts.markdown: *A cylinder has a definite lateral area and a definite volume which may be approximated as nearly as we please by taking the lateral areas and the volumes of successive inscribed or circumscribed prisms*.
excerpts.why: It states the fundamental assumption that lets a learner treat a cylinder's area and volume as limits of prism values.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The lateral area of a cylinder can be computed only in case the perimeter of a right section can be found, and this is possible by elementary methods only in case the right section is a circle.
excerpts.markdown: The lateral area of a cylinder can be computed only in case the perimeter of a right section can be found, and this is possible by elementary methods only in case the right section is a circle.
excerpts.why: It shows why circular cylinders are the case that elementary geometry can handle, which motivates the formulas that follow.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The moving line is the \emph{generator}, and the generator in any one of its positions is an \emph{element} of the surface.
excerpts.markdown: The moving line is the *generator*, and the generator in any one of its positions is an *element* of the surface.
excerpts.why: It gives the learner a clear mental picture of how a cylinder's surface is built by a sliding line.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: In this case $r = r_1 = r_2$, and $e = h$, and the formulas of corollaries~1 and~2 become identical.
excerpts.markdown: In this case $r = r_1 = r_2$, and $e = h$, and the formulas of corollaries 1 and 2 become identical.
excerpts.why: It shows the learner that the general volume formula reduces to the familiar right circular cylinder formula, tying the cases together.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: If a line through the fixed point moves so as to touch the boundary of the polygon and is made to traverse it completely, the line is said to generate a convex \emph{pyramidal surface}.
excerpts.markdown: If a line through the fixed point moves so as to touch the boundary of the polygon and is made to traverse it completely, the line is said to generate a convex *pyramidal surface*.
excerpts.why: It gives the learner the motion-based definition of a pyramidal surface, which makes the generator, element and vertex intelligible as parts of one picture.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The lateral area of a regular pyramid is equal to one half the product of its slant height and the perimeter of the base.
excerpts.markdown: The lateral area of a regular pyramid is equal to one half the product of its slant height and the perimeter of the base.
excerpts.why: It states the lateral area rule in words a learner can apply before reading the proof, linking slant height to surface area.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The volume of any pyramid is one third of the product of its base and altitude.
excerpts.markdown: The volume of any pyramid is one third of the product of its base and altitude.
excerpts.why: It is the central volume result for pyramids and the sentence a learner should be able to state and use.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: \textit{A pyramid has a definite volume which is less than the combined volume of any set of circumscribed prisms and greater than that of any set of inscribed prisms}.
excerpts.markdown: *A pyramid has a definite volume which is less than the combined volume of any set of circumscribed prisms and greater than that of any set of inscribed prisms*.
excerpts.why: It shows the book openly adopting an assumption about volume rather than proving it, so learners see where the argument's foundation lies.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The volume of a frustum of a pyramid is equal to the combined volumes of three pyramids whose common altitude is the same as that of the frustum, and the areas of whose bases are those of the upper and lower bases of the frustum and the mean proportional between these areas.
excerpts.markdown: The volume of a frustum of a pyramid is equal to the combined volumes of three pyramids whose common altitude is the same as that of the frustum, and the areas of whose bases are those of the upper and lower bases of the frustum and the mean proportional between these areas.
excerpts.why: It states the frustum volume result as a sum of pyramid volumes, a clear bridge from pyramids to frustums for a learner.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: This process may be repeated by doubling the number of planes drawn parallel to the base and thus doubling the number of inscribed or circumscribed prisms. By continuing in this way either set of prisms may be made to coincide as nearly as we please with the pyramid.
excerpts.markdown: This process may be repeated by doubling the number of planes drawn parallel to the base and thus doubling the number of inscribed or circumscribed prisms. By continuing in this way either set of prisms may be made to coincide as nearly as we please with the pyramid.
excerpts.why: It explains the limiting idea behind approximating a pyramid's volume by prisms, in the book's own old style of exhaustion.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: In this case every face is a triangle, and any one of them may be taken as the base.
excerpts.markdown: In this case every face is a triangle, and any one of them may be taken as the base.
excerpts.why: It warns learners that a tetrahedron has no privileged base, which avoids a common confusion when choosing the altitude.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: by rotating a right triangle $PMB$ about one of its legs, $PM$, as an axis.
excerpts.markdown: by rotating a right triangle $PMB$ about one of its legs, $PM$, as an axis.
excerpts.why: It gives a concrete rotation picture for generating a right circular cone, which a learner can visualise or model.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The circumscribed pyramids all have the same slant height as that of the cone, and in case of the inscribed pyramids, the slant height may be made to differ by as little as we please from that of the cone by making the number of faces great enough.
excerpts.markdown: The circumscribed pyramids all have the same slant height as that of the cone, and in case of the inscribed pyramids, the slant height may be made to differ by as little as we please from that of the cone by making the number of faces great enough.
excerpts.why: It shows a learner why the slant height of an approximating pyramid settles to that of the cone, the idea behind the lateral area argument.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: Evidently either of these processes may be repeated indefinitely and the surfaces of the inscribed or circumscribed pyramids may be made to lie as close to the surface of the cone as we please.
excerpts.markdown: Evidently either of these processes may be repeated indefinitely and the surfaces of the inscribed or circumscribed pyramids may be made to lie as close to the surface of the cone as we please.
